teile.einleitung: The Apocrypha are ancient Jewish and Christian writings that are not counted as part of the Bible, or not everywhere. Some stand in Catholic Bibles, others were never included in the Bible. Many of them have nevertheless strongly shaped art and belief.
wichtigste: The Greek word “apocryphal” means hidden.
Books such as Tobit, Judith and Jesus Sirach are called deuterocanonical writings by Catholics.
Luther did not rank them equal to scripture, but called them useful to read.
The Gospel of Thomas was found in 1945 at Nag Hammadi in Egypt.
It consists of 114 sayings of Jesus.
The names Joachim and Anna come from the Protoevangelium of James.
In the Ethiopian Orthodox Church the Book of Enoch is part of the Bible.

abschnitte.text: The Greek word **apocryphal** means **hidden**. Originally it meant writings that were not read in public in worship. Today it describes writings that do not belong to the **canon**. The canon is the fixed list of books that a church recognises as the Bible. Which books belong to it is not the same in all churches.

Books such as **Tobit**, **Judith** and **Jesus Sirach** belong to the Bible for the **Catholic** Church. It calls them **deuterocanonical writings**, that is, writings of the “second” part of the canon. In the Protestant tradition they are called the Apocrypha. **Martin Luther** placed them in his Bible of **1534** between the Old and New Testaments. He called them books that are not held equal to Holy Scripture, but are **useful and good to read**.

In **1945**, farmers near **Nag Hammadi** in Egypt found a jar with ancient books made of papyrus. In it was the only complete version of the **Gospel of Thomas**, in the **Coptic** language. It contains no account of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. Instead it strings together **114 sayings of Jesus**, which are called **logia**.

Some Apocrypha tell things that are not in the New Testament. The **Protoevangelium of James** from the **2nd century** tells of Mary's birth and childhood. From it come the names **Joachim** and **Anna** for Mary's parents. Saint Anne was later greatly venerated, and many churches and chapels bear her name.

The **Book of Enoch** survives in full only in the ancient Ethiopian language **Ge'ez**. In the **Ethiopian Orthodox Church** it is part of the Bible. In other churches it counts among the Apocrypha. Nevertheless, the **Letter of Jude** in the New Testament quotes a prophecy of Enoch, in verses 14 and 15. It corresponds to a passage in the first Book of Enoch.

gewusst: Parts of the Book of Enoch were also found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
The Ethiopian Bible includes more books than any other Christian Bible.

teile.einleitung: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Protestant theologian and pastor from Germany. He resisted the Nazi regime of Adolf Hitler. Shortly before the end of the war in 1945 he was executed in the Flossenbürg concentration camp.
wichtigste: Bonhoeffer was born in Breslau in 1906 and had a twin sister called Sabine.
His father Karl Bonhoeffer was a well-known psychiatrist in Berlin.
In 1930 and 1931 he studied in New York and got to know the congregations in Harlem.
He belonged to the Confessing Church and led a preachers' seminary in Finkenwalde.
His book “The Cost of Discipleship” appeared in 1937.
In prison at the end of 1944 he wrote the poem “By Gracious Powers”.
On 9 April 1945 he was murdered in the Flossenbürg concentration camp.

abschnitte.text: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was born in 1906 in **Breslau**, now Wrocław in Poland. He had a **twin sister** called **Sabine** and seven siblings altogether. His father **Karl Bonhoeffer** was a **psychiatrist** and professor. The family later moved to **Berlin**. Even as a teenager Dietrich decided to study theology.

Bonhoeffer studied theology and became a lecturer at the University of Berlin while still young. In 1930 and 1931 he studied at Union Theological Seminary in **New York**. At the Abyssinian Baptist Church in **Harlem** he got to know the services of the Black congregation. He was enthusiastic about the **spirituals** and saw how much these people suffered from racism.

After 1933 the “German Christians” wanted to adapt the Protestant church to Nazi ideology. The **Confessing Church**, to which Bonhoeffer belonged, resisted this. For it he led a **preachers' seminary** in **Finkenwalde**, where he trained young pastors. In 1937 his book **“The Cost of Discipleship”** appeared. In it he warns against “cheap grace”, which costs nothing and changes nothing.

Bonhoeffer rejected **National Socialism** from the start. During the war he had contact with men who wanted to **overthrow Hitler**. For them he also travelled abroad, including to **Switzerland**. In April 1943 he was arrested and put in prison in Berlin. On **9 April 1945**, a few weeks before the end of the war, he was murdered in the **Flossenbürg concentration camp** in Bavaria. He was 39 years old.

In December 1944, Bonhoeffer wrote the poem **“By Gracious Powers”** in prison. He sent it as a Christmas greeting to his family. In it he speaks of trust, even in a hard time. Today it is sung as a **hymn** in many churches, often at the turn of the year. His letters from prison were also later published and widely read.

gewusst: Bonhoeffer's letters from prison appeared after the war under the title “Letters and Papers from Prison”.
His sister Sabine had to flee to England with her husband from the Nazis.

teile.einleitung: Gregory the Great was Pope from **590 to 604** and is one of the most important popes of the early Middle Ages. He was a politician, monk, pastor and writer. He is regarded as one of the four great Doctors of the Church of the West.
wichtigste: Gregory the Great was Pope from 590 to 604.
Before that he was prefect of the city of Rome and then a monk.
In Constantinople he was the papal envoy at the imperial court.
In 596 he sent monks to convert the Anglo-Saxons in England.
He called himself “Servus servorum Dei”, servant of the servants of God.
His “Regula pastoralis” became a handbook for bishops.

abschnitte.text: Gregory came from a noble Roman family. Around 573 he was **prefect of the city of Rome**, the highest secular office in the city. After that he gave away his fortune, founded monasteries and became a **monk**. Around 579 Pope Pelagius II sent him as **apocrisiarius**, that is, papal envoy, to the imperial court in **Constantinople**. There he got to know the politics of the Eastern Roman Empire.

Gregory was elected Pope in **590** during a plague epidemic. He made sure that the people of Rome were supplied with grain. He called himself **“Servus servorum Dei”**, which means “servant of the servants of God”. The popes still bear this humble title today. Gregory died in Rome in **604**.

In **596** Gregory sent the monk **Augustine** with companions to the **Anglo-Saxons** in England. They landed in Kent in 597 and baptised King Æthelberht. Augustine became the first Archbishop of **Canterbury**. This mission was important for the spread of Christianity in England.

Gregory wrote many books. In the **“Dialogues”** there is the most important biography of Saint **Benedict of Nursia**. The **“Regula pastoralis”** describes how a bishop should live and preach. In the Middle Ages it became a handbook for bishops and pastors. **Gregorian chant** is also named after Gregory.

A legend tells of a penitential procession against the plague in the year 590. During it the **Archangel Michael** is said to have appeared above the tomb of the Emperor Hadrian and sheathed his sword. This was taken as a sign that the plague was coming to an end. Since then the building has been called **Castel Sant'Angelo**, the Castle of the Holy Angel. On its top stands a figure of an angel to this day.

gewusst: Almost everything we know about Saint Benedict comes from Gregory's “Dialogues”.
The “Regula pastoralis” was translated into Old English at an early date.

teile.einleitung: The Wars of Kappel were two short wars in the Swiss Confederation in the years 1529 and 1531. They were about faith: Zurich was Reformed, the Central Swiss places stayed Catholic. They are named after Kappel am Albis in the canton of Zurich.
wichtigste: There were two Wars of Kappel, in 1529 and 1531.
Zurich was on the Reformed side.
Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne and Zug fought on the Catholic side.
In the First War of Kappel came the peaceful Kappel Milk Soup.
Before the Second War of Kappel, Zurich imposed a food blockade.
Zwingli lost his life in the Battle of Kappel in 1531.
The Second Peace of Kappel let every place decide its own faith.

abschnitte.text: In the 1520s **Huldrych Zwingli** introduced the **Reformation** in Zurich. Bern and other places also became Reformed. The five places **Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne and Zug** stayed Catholic. The dispute became ever fiercer, especially in the territories that several places administered together. So came the two **Wars of Kappel**.

In the **First War of Kappel in 1529** the armies faced each other near Kappel. But no battle took place. The legend tells that soldiers from both sides ate a **milk soup** together: one side brought the milk, the other the bread. This scene is called the **Kappel Milk Soup**. After that the parties concluded the First Peace of Kappel.

The peace did not last long. Zurich put pressure on the Catholic places with a **food blockade**, so they no longer received grain and salt. In **1531** the Catholic places attacked. In the **Battle of Kappel** they won, and **Zwingli** lost his life. He had accompanied the Zurich troops as a field chaplain.

After the war the places concluded the **Second Peace of Kappel**. It determined that **every place could choose its own faith**. After that the Reformation could hardly spread any further in the Confederation. Switzerland stayed divided for a long time into Reformed and Catholic areas. Even so, the Confederation held together.

**Kappel am Albis** lies in the **canton of Zurich**, near the border with the canton of Zug. Well known is the former **Kappel Abbey** with its church. Today it is a place for meeting and quiet. Nearby a monument recalls Zwingli and the battle of 1531.

gewusst: The Kappel Milk Soup is still seen today as a symbol that Swiss disputes can also be settled peacefully.
A painting by Albert Anker shows the Kappel Milk Soup.

teile.einleitung: Jeremiah is one of the great prophets of the Old Testament. He lived in a hard time, when the Babylonian Empire conquered Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple.
wichtigste: Jeremiah was active in the kingdom of Judah before and during the conquest of Jerusalem.
The Babylonian Empire destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple.
His scribe Baruch wrote down his words.
The word “jeremiad” for a long speech of complaint comes from his name.
Traditionally the Book of Lamentations is also attributed to him.

abschnitte.text: Jeremiah lived in the kingdom of **Judah** in the 7th and 6th centuries BC. He warned the people and the kings: if they did not turn away from false gods and live justly, disaster would come. Nobody wanted to hear this message. Jeremiah was therefore mocked, persecuted and at times imprisoned. He often complained about his hard task.

In his time the **Babylonian Empire** under King Nebuchadnezzar II became very powerful. It **conquered Jerusalem** and in 587 or 586 BC destroyed the **Temple**. Many people were taken away to Babylon; this period is called the **Babylonian Exile**. Jeremiah at first stayed in the land. In a letter he encouraged those taken away to trust in God even in a foreign land.

Jeremiah's words were written down on a scroll by his scribe **Baruch**. A king had this scroll burned, but Baruch wrote everything down again. Traditionally the **Book of Lamentations** is also attributed to Jeremiah, a book of mourning songs about the destroyed Jerusalem. Because Jeremiah complained so much, a long, wailing speech is still called a **jeremiad** today.

gewusst: The Book of Jeremiah is among the longest books of the Bible.
Jeremiah is sometimes called the “weeping prophet”.

teile.einleitung: The Rule of Saint Benedict is a guide to life in a monastery. Benedict of Nursia wrote it in the 6th century. To this day Benedictines and other members of religious orders live by this rule.
wichtigste: Benedict of Nursia wrote the rule in the 6th century.
Around 529 he founded the monastery of Monte Cassino in Italy.
The rule consists of 73 chapters.
It is often linked with the motto “Ora et labora”.
The head of a monastery is called an abbot.
With “stabilitas loci”, monks promise to stay in the same monastery.

abschnitte.text: **Benedict of Nursia** founded the monastery of **Monte Cassino** in Italy around 529. For his monks he wrote a rule in the **6th century**. It consists of **73 chapters**. It says how the monks should pray, work, eat, sleep and treat one another. The rule is strict, but it also calls for moderation and consideration for the weak, the sick and the old.

The Rule of Saint Benedict is often linked with the Latin motto **“Ora et labora”**, in English “Pray and work”. It does not appear in the rule in these exact words, but it sums it up well. The day is divided into fixed times. Several times a day the monks meet for the **Liturgy of the Hours**. In between they work, read and learn.

At the head of a monastery stands the **abbot**. The word comes from the Aramaic “Abba”, father. The abbot is meant to lead the monks like a good father. The monks owe him **obedience**. But he should discuss important decisions together with the community. He must try to be fair to every monk.

A special promise is **“stabilitas loci”**, stability of place. The monk promises to **stay in the same monastery** all his life. In this way a firm community arises, like a family. The rule also demands that **guests** be received kindly, as if Christ himself were visiting.

The Rule of Saint Benedict spread across the whole of Europe in the Middle Ages. In Switzerland too there are well-known Benedictine monasteries. The best known is **Einsiedeln** in the canton of **Schwyz**, a great place of pilgrimage. Other Benedictine monasteries are, for example, Engelberg and Disentis. Some of them also run schools.

gewusst: The rule allowed the monks a certain amount of wine each day, but recommended moderation.
Benedictine nuns, too, live by the same rule.

teile.einleitung: Gabriel is one of the best-known angels of the Bible. He is regarded as a **messenger of God** who brings important news to people. He is especially well known because he announced to Mary that she would be the mother of Jesus.
wichtigste: Gabriel is an archangel, that is, a particularly important angel.
He brought Mary the message that she would be the mother of Jesus.
According to his words, the child was to be given the name Jesus.
Gabriel also announced the birth of John the Baptist.
The feast of the Annunciation is celebrated on 25 March.
In Islam too, Gabriel is an important angel.

abschnitte.text: The word angel comes from the Greek word for **messenger**. In the Bible, angels deliver messages from God. Gabriel is called an **archangel**, which means that he is one of the particularly important angels. His name is often translated as “God is strong” or “hero of God”. Already in the Old Testament, in the Book of Daniel, Gabriel explains his visions to the prophet.

In the **Gospel of Luke**, God sends Gabriel to Mary in the town of Nazareth. The angel greets her and tells her that she will be the mother of a son. The child is to be called **Jesus** and will be called the Son of God. Mary is frightened at first, but then says yes to God's plan. This scene is called the **Annunciation**.

The angel's message is recalled by the feast of the **Annunciation** on 25 March. This is exactly nine months before Christmas on 25 December. Many famous painters have painted the Annunciation. Usually Gabriel is shown with wings and a lily in his hand; the lily stands for purity.

In the Gospel of Luke, Gabriel brings a second piece of news. He appears to the priest **Zechariah** in the Temple in Jerusalem. He announces to him that he and his wife Elizabeth will have a son, even though they are already old. This son is **John the Baptist**, who will later baptise Jesus.

In **Islam** too, Gabriel is very important; in Arabic he is called **Jibril**. According to Muslim belief he brought the revelations of the Quran to the Prophet Muhammad. This means that Gabriel appears in Judaism, Christianity and Islam. In the Catholic Church he is celebrated on 29 September together with the archangels Michael and Raphael.

gewusst: The prayer “Hail Mary” begins with the words with which Gabriel greeted Mary.
In art Gabriel often carries a staff or a scroll as a sign of the messenger.

teile.einleitung: Iconoclasm means the removal and destruction of images from churches. In the Reformation this happened in many towns, including in Switzerland. That is why Reformed churches today usually look plain inside.
wichtigste: In iconoclasm, images and statues were removed from churches.
The Reformed appealed to the commandment “You shall not make for yourself an image”.
In Zurich the images were removed from the churches in 1524.
In Basel a violent iconoclasm broke out in 1529.
Often the organs were removed too.
Reformed churches in Switzerland are usually plain inside.

abschnitte.text: The reformers criticised the fact that people venerated pictures of saints and statues. They appealed to the biblical commandment “**You shall not make for yourself an image**”. For them, **God's word** alone should stand at the centre. In their view, images distracted from it. Expensive images would also have cost money that would better have been given to the poor.

As early as **1522** the theologian **Andreas Karlstadt** pushed for the removal of images in **Wittenberg**. **Martin Luther** was in hiding at the Wartburg at this time. When he came back, he stopped the unrest. Luther did not consider images forbidden, so long as they were not worshipped. That is why Lutheran churches often still have images and altars.

In **Zurich**, **Huldrych Zwingli** worked for the Reformation. In **1524** the images were removed from the churches in an orderly way, by decision of the council. In **Basel** a violent iconoclasm broke out in **1529**: an angry crowd destroyed many images in the Minster and in other churches. After that the Reformation was introduced there. In Bern and other places too, images were removed.

In many Reformed churches the **organs** were also removed. Zwingli thought that in worship people should listen to the word, not to music. Only later did organs and singing return to the Reformed churches. Today Reformed churches in Switzerland usually look **plain inside, without pictures of saints**. What matters are the pulpit and the communion table.

gewusst: Some works of art were hidden or sold at that time and have survived to this day in that way.
As early as the 8th and 9th centuries there was a great dispute over images in the Byzantine Empire, the Iconoclastic Controversy.

teile.einleitung: The Confessio Helvetica posterior is an important statement of faith of the Reformed churches. In English it is called the Second Helvetic Confession. It was written by Heinrich Bullinger, Zwingli's successor in Zurich.
wichtigste: The author was Heinrich Bullinger of Zurich.
The confession came into being around 1561/62 and was printed in 1566.
It was published at the request of Elector Frederick III of the Palatinate.
“Posterior” means “the later one”; there is also an older confession of 1536 from Basel.
In Hungary it is still a central confession of the Reformed today.
A famous sentence says: “The preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.”

abschnitte.text: After Zwingli's death, **Heinrich Bullinger** led the Zurich church for over 40 years. Around 1561/62 he wrote a detailed **testimony of faith** for himself. He wanted to set down what he believed. At first it was not intended for the public at all. A few years later it became one of the best-known confessions of the Reformed churches.

The Elector **Frederick III of the Palatinate** was inclined to the Reformed faith. For the Imperial Diet of **1566** he needed a confession to justify his faith. Bullinger placed his text at his disposal. In the same year the confession was printed. Many Reformed churches in Switzerland adopted it.

abschnitte.titel: The first and the second confession
abschnitte.text: The Latin word **posterior** means “the later one”. For there was already an older confession, the **Confessio Helvetica prior**. Theologians from several Reformed cities had written it in **Basel** in 1536. The later confession is much more detailed. That is why it is called the **Second Helvetic Confession** in English.

abschnitte.titel: The sermon as the Word of God
abschnitte.text: In the first chapter stands the famous sentence: “The preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.” In Latin it reads “Praedicatio verbi Dei est verbum Dei”. This means that when the Bible is interpreted rightly, God speaks to people through the **sermon**. That is why the sermon is so important in Reformed services.

The confession became known far beyond Switzerland. In **Hungary** the Synod of Debrecen adopted it in 1567. The Reformed Church in Hungary still refers to it today. It was also recognised in other countries, such as Poland and Scotland. In this way it united Reformed Christians all over Europe.

gewusst: Heinrich Bullinger wrote so many letters that around 12,000 of them survive today.
The confession was written in Latin so that scholars all over Europe could read it.

teile.einleitung: Augustine of Hippo was a bishop and scholar in North Africa. He lived from 354 to 430 and is regarded as one of the most important thinkers of Christianity. His books are still read today.
wichtigste: Augustine was born in 354 in Thagaste in present-day Algeria.
His mother Monica prayed for a long time for his conversion.
Before his conversion he followed Manichaeism for about nine years.
In 387 he was baptised in Milan by Bishop Ambrose.
For over 30 years he was Bishop of Hippo Regius, also in present-day Algeria.
His best-known works are the “Confessions” and “The City of God”.

abschnitte.text: Augustine was born in 354 in **Thagaste**, a town in present-day **Algeria**. North Africa then belonged to the Roman Empire. His father was not a Christian, but his mother **Monica** was a committed Christian. Augustine studied in Carthage and was very gifted. As a young man he searched for the truth and joined **Manichaeism**, a widespread teaching at the time, for about nine years.

Augustine became a **teacher of the art of speaking**, also called rhetoric. He worked in Rome and then in **Milan**. There he heard the sermons of Bishop **Ambrose**, which impressed him greatly. After a long struggle he turned to Christianity. In the year **387** Ambrose baptised him in Milan. His mother Monica lived to see this.

Back in Africa, Augustine became a priest and soon Bishop of **Hippo Regius**, a port town in present-day Algeria. He held this office for over 30 years, until his death in 430. He preached, wrote letters and argued with other scholars about questions of faith. With companions he lived in a monastic community.

In the **“Confessions”**, Augustine tells his own life and his conversion. It is one of the first books in which a person writes so openly about his inner life. In **“The City of God”** he contrasts the state of God with the earthly state. He wrote this great work after Rome had been conquered in the year 410.

Augustine shaped the thinking of the Church for many centuries. He is regarded as one of the **Church Fathers**. The **Order of Saint Augustine** appeals to a rule that comes from him. **Martin Luther** later belonged to this order. In this way Augustine influenced both Catholic and Protestant theologians.

gewusst: A well-known sentence from the “Confessions” runs, roughly: “Our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
Augustine left behind over 100 works and many hundreds of letters and sermons.

teile.einleitung: Karl Barth was a Swiss Reformed theologian. He lived from 1886 to 1968 and came from Basel. He is regarded as one of the most important Protestant theologians of the 20th century.
wichtigste: Karl Barth was pastor in Safenwil in Aargau from 1911 to 1921.
In 1919 he became known through his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans.
The early Barth belongs to Dialectical Theology.
In 1935 he lost his professorship in Bonn because he refused the unconditional oath to Hitler.
After that he taught at the University of Basel until 1962.
His unfinished main work is called “Church Dogmatics”.
Barth revered Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.

abschnitte.text: Karl Barth was born in **Basel in 1886**. After his studies he became a pastor. From **1911 to 1921** he worked in the Aargau parish of **Safenwil**. There he saw the hardship of the workers in the factories and stood up for them. During this time he began to read the Bible in a completely new way.

In **1919** Barth published a commentary on the **Epistle to the Romans** of the Apostle Paul. The book made him known at a stroke. Barth stressed that God is wholly other than human beings and can only reveal himself. This direction is called **Dialectical Theology**. Soon Barth became a professor at German universities.

In Germany **Hitler** came to power in 1933. Barth belonged to the **Confessing Church**, which resisted the influence of the National Socialists on the church. He was the main author of the **Barmen Theological Declaration** of 1934. Because he **refused the unconditional oath to Hitler**, he lost his professorship in Bonn in **1935**. He returned to Switzerland and taught at the **University of Basel** until **1962**.

Barth's main work is the **Church Dogmatics**. In it he explains the Christian faith in detail. The work comprises over **9,000 pages** and nevertheless remained **unfinished**. In 1934 Barth argued fiercely with the Zurich theologian **Emil Brunner** about natural theology. His reply bore the short title **“No!”**.

Barth loved the music of **Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart** very much. He is said to have listened to Mozart every morning before he began work. For the composer's 200th birthday in **1956** he wrote a piece of his own for him. Barth died in **Basel in 1968**.

gewusst: Barth was one of the theologians who took an early and clear stand against National Socialism.
The Church Dogmatics is one of the most extensive theological works of the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: From 1309 to 1377 the popes did not live in Rome but in Avignon in southern France. This period is called the Avignon Papacy. Seven popes ruled from there in this time.
wichtigste: The popes resided in Avignon from 1309 to 1377.
Pope Clement V moved his seat to Avignon in 1309.
The French king Philip IV the Fair put the papacy under heavy pressure.
Seven popes ruled from Avignon.
Petrarch called this time a “Babylonian captivity”.
Catherine of Siena urged Gregory XI to return to Rome.

abschnitte.text: Around 1300 the pope and the French king **Philip IV the Fair** quarrelled fiercely over power. Philip wanted to control the Church in his country himself. He put the papacy under heavy pressure. After that a Frenchman, **Clement V**, was elected pope. He did not go to Rome but moved his seat **to Avignon in 1309**.

Between 1309 and 1377, **seven popes** ruled from Avignon. There they had a huge **Palace of the Popes** built, one of the largest Gothic fortresses. Avignon became an important centre of administration, art and trade. Many cardinals were French. Critics thought the pope was too much under the influence of the French king.

Under Clement V the **Order of the Templars** was dissolved. The Templars were a powerful order of knights from the time of the Crusades. King Philip IV had them persecuted, partly because he wanted their wealth. In **1312** the **Council of Vienne** dissolved the order. This shows how strongly the king influenced the Church.

The Italian poet **Francesco Petrarch** called the stay in Avignon a **“Babylonian captivity”**. In doing so he recalled the time when the people of Israel had to live in Babylon. The mystic **Catherine of Siena** wrote letters to Pope **Gregory XI** and urged him to return. In **1377** Gregory XI did indeed move back to Rome.

Soon after the return, in 1378, a split occurred: two, later even three, popes claimed the office. This time is called the **Western Schism**. Only the **Council of Constance** on Lake Constance ended the split, in the year 1417. The standing of the papacy had suffered greatly in this period.

gewusst: The Palace of the Popes and the old town of Avignon are part of UNESCO World Heritage today.
Avignon remained in the possession of the popes until 1791.

teile.einleitung: Fasnacht, or carnival, is a cheerful time before Lent. With masks, costumes and loud music, people celebrate with abandon. In Switzerland the carnivals in Basel and Lucerne are especially well known.
wichtigste: After carnival, Lent begins.
Lent begins on Ash Wednesday and lasts until Easter.
The loud music groups are called Guggenmusiken.
The Basel Morgestraich begins at 4 o'clock in the morning.
The masks at the Basel carnival are called Larven.
The Lucerne carnival begins on Schmutziger Donnerstag, Dirty Thursday.

abschnitte.text: Carnival is linked to the church year. After it, **Lent** begins. It starts on **Ash Wednesday** and lasts until **Easter**. In the past, people gave up meat, eggs and fat during Lent. Before that, they wanted to celebrate and eat properly one more time.

Typical of the Swiss carnival are the **Guggenmusiken**. These are loud music groups with trumpets, trombones and big drums. They play slightly off key on purpose. The members wear colourful, often homemade costumes and masks.

The **Basel carnival** begins on the Monday after Ash Wednesday with the **Morgestraich** at **4 o'clock in the morning**. Then the lights go out in the city. The groups move through the dark lanes with large, glowing lanterns, piccolos and drums. In Basel the masks are called **Larven**. The carnival lasts three days.

In **Lucerne** the carnival begins on **Schmutziger Donnerstag**, that is, the Thursday before Ash Wednesday. It starts early in the morning with a loud bang. Then Guggenmusiken and people in costume move through the old town. There are also parades in many other places in Switzerland.
In Switzerland, **Fasnachtschüechli** belong to carnival. These are thin, deep-fried flat pastries dusted with icing sugar. In Basel people also like to eat flour soup and onion tart.

gewusst: Since 2017 the Basel carnival has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.
The word “schmutzig” (dirty) in Schmutziger Donnerstag comes from the old word “Schmotz” for fat.

teile.einleitung: Gregorian chant is the traditional singing of the Catholic Church. It is sung in **unison**, without instruments and in **Latin**. It is named after Pope **Gregory the Great**.
wichtigste: The chant is named after Pope Gregory the Great.
It is sung in unison and without instruments.
The language is traditionally Latin.
In the Middle Ages the melodies were written down with neumes.
In St Gallen lies one of the oldest chant manuscripts with neumes.
The monastery of Solesmes revived the chant in the 19th century.

abschnitte.text: In Gregorian chant everyone sings the **same melody**; this is called **unison**. There are no instruments and no accompaniment. The texts mostly come from the Bible, especially from the Psalms. It is sung in **Latin**, the old language of the Church. The name recalls Pope Gregory the Great, even though the chant grew over many centuries.

In the Middle Ages it was mainly **monks and nuns** in the monasteries who sang the chant. They prayed together several times a day, and singing was part of it. The melodies are in the **church modes**. These are old scales that sound different from our major and minor today. That is why the chant sounds calm and solemn.

At first the melodies were learned by heart. Later they were written down with **neumes**, small signs above the text. They show whether the melody rises or falls. In the **Abbey Library of St Gallen** lies the **Cantatorium**, one of the oldest surviving chant manuscripts with neumes. The monastery of St Gallen was an important centre of chant in the Middle Ages.

Later **square notation** arose, with square-shaped notes. It is usually written on **four lines**, not on five as is usual today. In the 19th century the monks of the Benedictine abbey of **Solesmes** in France studied the old manuscripts. They gave the chant new life. To this day it is sung in many monasteries.

gewusst: The Abbey Library of St Gallen is part of a UNESCO World Heritage site together with the abbey precinct.
In the 1990s, a CD of Gregorian chant by Spanish monks became a worldwide bestseller.

teile.einleitung: The Old Testament is the first and larger part of the Christian Bible. It contains stories, laws, prayers and the words of prophets from many centuries. For the most part it corresponds to the holy scripture of Judaism, the Tanakh.
wichtigste: The Old Testament is the first part of the Christian Bible.
In Protestant Bibles it has 39 books.
Catholic Bibles also contain some late writings such as Tobit and Judith.
Judaism calls its holy scripture the Tanakh.
The word “testament” here means covenant.
In most Christian Bibles the Old Testament ends with the Book of Malachi.

abschnitte.titel: The covenant between God and people
abschnitte.text: The Christian Bible has two parts: the **Old** and the **New Testament**. The Latin word **testamentum** translates the Hebrew and Greek word for **covenant**. What is meant is the covenant between God and people. The Old Testament tells of God's covenant with the people of **Israel**. It was written for the most part in **Hebrew**.

Judaism calls its holy scripture the **Tanakh**. The name is formed from the initial letters of its three parts: **Torah** (instruction), **Nevi'im** (prophets) and **Ketuvim** (writings). The Tanakh corresponds for the most part to the Old Testament. The **Talmud**, by contrast, is a later collection of interpretations and is not part of the Bible.

The Old Testament is really a whole **library**. In **Protestant** Bibles it counts **39 books**, as many as the Hebrew Bible. There are history books, laws, prayers such as the **Psalms**, wisdom books and **books of the prophets**. At the beginning stands the Book of **Genesis**, with the story of creation, of Adam and Eve and of Abraham.

Catholic Bibles also contain some **late writings**, for example **Tobit** and **Judith**. These writings have been handed down mainly in the **Greek** translation of the Old Testament. Catholics count them as part of the Bible. Protestant Bibles often do not print them at all, or only in an **appendix**. There they are called the **Apocrypha**.

The books do not stand in the same order in all Bibles. In **Christian** Bibles the books of the prophets come at the end of the Old Testament. The last of them is the little prophetic book of **Malachi**. In this way the Old Testament leads directly over to the New Testament. In the Jewish Tanakh, by contrast, the Writings come at the end.

gewusst: The longest book of the Old Testament by chapters is the Book of Psalms, with 150 psalms.
Some parts of the Old Testament, for example in the Book of Daniel, are written in Aramaic.

teile.einleitung: Eternity Sunday is the last Sunday of the church year. In Protestant churches, people remember the dead on this day. It is therefore also called the Sunday of the Dead.
wichtigste: Eternity Sunday is on the last Sunday before the 1st Sunday of Advent.
It always falls between 20 and 26 November.
Another name is Totensonntag, the Sunday of the Dead.
It is mainly found in Protestant churches.
King Frederick William III introduced the Sunday of the Dead in Prussia in 1816.
On the same Sunday Catholics celebrate Christ the King Sunday.

abschnitte.text: The church year begins with the 1st Sunday of Advent. The Sunday before it is therefore the last Sunday of the church year. This is **Eternity Sunday**. It always falls on a day between **20 and 26 November**.

Another name is **Totensonntag** (Sunday of the Dead). In many **Protestant churches**, the names of the people who died in the past year are read out on this day. Often a candle is lit for each one. Many families visit the graves. The name **Eternity Sunday** expresses the **hope of eternal life with God**.

King **Frederick William III** introduced the Sunday of the Dead in Prussia in **1816**. He wanted to remember those who had fallen in the wars against Napoleon. His wife, Queen Louise, had also died a few years earlier. Other Protestant churches later took over the day.

The hymn of the week for Eternity Sunday is **“Wake, O Wake! With Tidings Thrilling”** (Wachet auf, ruft uns die Stimme) by **Philipp Nicolai**. It tells of waiting for Christ. The services are about grief, comfort and hope. In Switzerland many Reformed congregations also hold a memorial service on this Sunday.

abschnitte.titel: The Catholic Christ the King Sunday
abschnitte.text: In the Catholic Church, the same Sunday is **Christ the King Sunday**. It celebrates Jesus Christ as king of the world. Catholics, by contrast, remember the dead mainly on All Souls' Day on 2 November.

gewusst: Johann Sebastian Bach wrote a well-known cantata on the hymn “Wachet auf, ruft uns die Stimme”.
Philipp Nicolai wrote the hymn around 1599, when a serious illness was killing many people in his town.

teile.einleitung: On Good Friday, Christians think of the death of Jesus on the cross. It is the Friday before Easter and one of the most important days in the church year. It is a quiet day of mourning, but also of hope for Easter.
wichtigste: On Good Friday, Christians remember the death of Jesus.
The old word “Kar” in German means mourning or lament.
Jesus died on the cross on the hill of Golgotha.
Pontius Pilate sentenced Jesus to death.
Simon of Cyrene helped Jesus carry the cross.
A Way of the Cross usually has 14 stations.
In Mendrisio TI and Romont FR there are special customs.

abschnitte.text: **Good Friday** is the Friday before Easter. On this day Christians remember the **suffering** and **death of Jesus** on the cross. The German word for Good Friday, Karfreitag, contains the old word **“Kar”**, which comes from Old High German and means **mourning** or lament. In many churches the bells and the organ are silent. For the Reformed, Good Friday was for a long time one of the highest holy days.

The Gospels tell that Jesus was arrested in Jerusalem. The Roman governor **Pontius Pilate** sentenced him to death on the **cross**. Jesus had to carry the cross himself. Because he was too weak, **Simon of Cyrene** helped him. Jesus was crucified on the hill of **Golgotha** outside the city and died there.

Many Christians pray the **Way of the Cross** on Good Friday. It usually has **14 stations**. Each station shows a moment from the journey of Jesus, from the condemnation to the tomb. Such Ways of the Cross can be found on the walls of many Catholic churches. Some also lead up a hill outside, often to a chapel.

In **Mendrisio** in the canton of **Ticino**, famous **processions** take place on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday. Many people in costume walk through the old town, which is decorated with illuminated pictures. These processions are part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage. In **Romont FR**, on Good Friday, **women in mourning** in black clothes walk silently through the streets. They carry cushions with symbols of the sufferings of Jesus.

Good Friday is one of the three holy days before Easter. For Christians the story does not end with death. On **Easter Sunday** they celebrate the **resurrection** of Jesus. So Good Friday is quiet, but also a day of hope. In most cantons it is a **public holiday**.

gewusst: Many people traditionally eat no meat on Good Friday, but fish.
The name Golgotha means “place of the skull”.

teile.einleitung: Corpus Christi (Fronleichnam) is a Catholic festival. The faithful celebrate that Jesus Christ is present in the host. Festive processions through the streets are typical.
wichtigste: “Fronleichnam” means “body of the Lord”.
The feast is 60 days after Easter Sunday, always on a Thursday.
Pope Urban IV introduced it for the whole Church in 1264.
In the procession the host is carried in the monstrance.
The priest walks under a canopy.
In the canton of Lucerne, Corpus Christi is a public holiday.

abschnitte.text: The word **Fronleichnam** comes from Middle High German. “Fron” means lord, “lichnam” means living body. So Fronleichnam means **“body of the Lord”**. What is meant is the consecrated **host**. Catholics believe that Jesus Christ is present in it.

The feast is **60 days after Easter Sunday**. It always falls on a **Thursday**. The Thursday recalls Maundy Thursday, when Jesus celebrated the last meal. Because Easter is on a different day every year, the date of Corpus Christi also changes. It falls in May or June.

Pope **Urban IV** introduced the feast for the whole Church in **1264**. It had been proposed by the nun Juliana of Liège in Belgium. In the Middle Ages the feast quickly became popular. In the Reformation the Protestant churches rejected it.

In the **procession** the faithful walk through the streets praying and singing. The priest carries the host in the **monstrance**. This is a precious vessel for display, often in the shape of a golden sun. Helpers carry a **canopy**, a cloth awning, over him. In some villages people lay **carpets of flowers** on the streets. They are made of many coloured blossoms and form patterns and pictures.

In Switzerland, Corpus Christi is a **public holiday** in several cantons with a Catholic tradition, for example in the canton of **Lucerne**. There, processions take place in many municipalities, often with brass bands, traditional costumes and flags. In cantons with a Reformed tradition, Corpus Christi is a normal working day.

gewusst: The word “monstrance” comes from the Latin “monstrare”, which means to show.
In Appenzell Innerrhoden, many people in traditional costume walk in the procession on Corpus Christi.

teile.einleitung: Gospel is a kind of Christian music that arose in **African American churches in the USA**. The English word gospel means **good news**, as in the Gospels. Gospel is powerful, joyful and invites people to sing and clap along.
wichtigste: Gospel arose in African American churches in the USA.
Gospel means the good news of the Gospels.
Its forerunners were the spirituals of enslaved African Americans.
Typical is call and response between a lead singer and the choir.
Mahalia Jackson was called the “Queen of Gospel”.
“Oh Happy Day” became a worldwide hit in 1969.

abschnitte.text: The first **spirituals** were sung by **enslaved African Americans** in the USA. In their songs they combined Bible stories with the hope of freedom. A well-known example is **“Go Down Moses”**. It tells how Moses says to Pharaoh: “Let my people go”. For the singers it was also a song about their own situation.

From **1871** the **Fisk Jubilee Singers** went on concert tours. This was a choir of Fisk University in **Nashville**, a college for African American students. They sang spirituals in the USA and in Europe. With the money they earned they supported their university. In this way spirituals became known worldwide.

Typical of gospel is **call and response**. A lead singer sings a line, and the choir answers. There is often clapping, and the congregation sings along. Gospel developed in the early 20th century and also took in elements of blues and jazz. Today there are also many gospel choirs in Switzerland.

The singer **Mahalia Jackson** was called the “Queen of Gospel”. She also sang at events of the civil rights movement in the USA. In **1969** the song **“Oh Happy Day”** by the Edwin Hawkins Singers became a worldwide hit. Many well-known pop and soul stars began their careers in the church choir.

gewusst: Fisk University still exists today, and the Fisk Jubilee Singers still perform.
Many soul singers first learned to sing in the gospel choir of their church.

teile.einleitung: The Franciscans are a Catholic order. Its founder is Francis of Assisi, who lived in Italy around 1200. The brothers live simply, in poverty and in the service of people.
wichtigste: Francis of Assisi founded the Franciscan order.
The Franciscans belong to the mendicant orders.
Pope Innocent III permitted their way of life around 1209.
The Poor Clares are the nuns following Clare of Assisi.
Francis wrote the Canticle of the Sun and in 1223 re-enacted the Nativity at Greccio.
The Capuchins arose in the 16th century as a reform branch.

abschnitte.text: **Francis of Assisi** gave up his wealth and lived as poor as Jesus. Soon other young men followed him. Around **1209** they went to Rome. Pope **Innocent III** permitted their way of life. In this way the **Franciscan order** arose. The brothers also call themselves “Friars Minor”, “lesser brothers”, because they want to be humble.

The Franciscans belong to the **mendicant orders**. The brothers originally owned nothing. They lived from their work and from what people gave them. They did not live secluded but in the towns among the people. They preached and helped the poor and the sick. Typical is their brown habit with a cord as a belt.

abschnitte.titel: Canticle of the Sun and crib
abschnitte.text: In the **Canticle of the Sun**, Francis praised sun, moon and water as brothers and sisters. The song shows the Franciscans' love of the whole of creation. In 1223 Francis re-enacted the **Nativity scene** at **Greccio** with people and animals. The Franciscans did a great deal to make cribs popular.

**Clare of Assisi** was a friend and follower of Francis. She founded an order for women. The nuns are named after her **Poor Clares**. They mostly live in convents, pray a great deal and rarely leave the convent.

In the **16th century** a reform branch of the Franciscans arose: the **Capuchins**. They wanted to live even more strictly after the example of Francis. They get their name from the long, pointed hood. In Switzerland the Capuchins are especially widespread, with Capuchin monasteries, for example, in Lucerne, Rapperswil and Wil.

gewusst: The drink cappuccino is named after the brown colour of the Capuchin habits.
The Franciscans are among the largest orders of the Catholic Church.

teile.einleitung: Elijah is a great prophet in the Old Testament. He worked to make sure that the people of Israel believed only in God and not in the god Baal. The Bible tells many wondrous stories about him.
wichtigste: Elijah announced a long drought without rain.
At the brook, ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning and in the evening.
For a poor widow, the flour and the oil never ran out.
On Mount Carmel he stood against the prophets of Baal, and fire fell from heaven.
In the desert an angel brought him bread and water.
God did not show himself to him in the storm, but in a gentle breath of wind.
In the end Elijah went up to heaven in a chariot of fire.

abschnitte.text: Elijah lived in the time of King **Ahab**, who also had the god **Baal** worshipped. Elijah announced that for a long time there would be **no rain**. Then he hid by a brook. God sent **ravens**, which brought him **bread and meat** in the morning and in the evening. When the brook dried up, Elijah moved on.

Elijah came to a poor **widow**. She had only a little **flour** and **oil** left for herself and her son. Even so, she first baked a loaf for Elijah. From then on her jar of flour and her jug of oil did not run empty for as long as the drought lasted. Only after about **three years** did rain come again.

On **Mount Carmel** it was to be shown who the true God is. The prophets of Baal and Elijah each prepared a sacrifice without lighting a fire. The prophets of Baal called out all day in vain. When Elijah prayed, **fire fell from heaven** and burned up his sacrifice. Then the people cried out that God is the true God.

abschnitte.titel: God in a gentle breath of wind
abschnitte.text: After that Elijah had to flee from Queen Jezebel. Exhausted, he slept in the desert under a bush. An **angel** woke him and gave him **bread and water**. Later, at Mount Horeb, a storm came, then an earthquake and a fire. But God was not in them. Then came a **soft, gentle breath of wind**, and God was in that.

Elijah had a pupil called **Elisha**, who became his successor. As the two were travelling together, a **chariot of fire** with horses of fire appeared. Elijah went up to heaven in a **whirlwind**. Elisha took up Elijah's cloak and carried on his work.

gewusst: At the Jewish festival of Passover, a cup is placed on the table for Elijah, because people hope for his return.
The composer Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy wrote a great oratorio called “Elijah”.

teile.einleitung: Saint Christopher is a saint about whom there is a well-known legend. He is said to have carried the infant Jesus on his shoulders across a river. That is why he is regarded as the patron saint of travellers.
wichtigste: The name Christopher comes from Greek and means “Christ-bearer”.
According to legend, Christopher was a giant.
At first he wanted to serve the most powerful lord in the world.
He carried people on his shoulders across a river, once even the infant Jesus.
The child became heavy because he carried the whole world and its Creator.
Christopher is regarded as the patron saint of travellers.
In the past, huge pictures of Christopher were painted on church walls.

abschnitte.titel: Searching for the most powerful lord
abschnitte.text: The legend tells of a very big and strong man, almost a **giant**. He wanted to serve only the **most powerful lord** in the world. First he served a king, then he noticed that others were more powerful. In the end a hermit advised him to serve Christ by carrying people across a dangerous river. This story is found in the famous medieval collection of legends, the **Golden Legend** (Legenda aurea).

In the water, Christopher leaned on a large **staff**. One night a small child asked him to carry it across. In the middle of the river the child became heavier and heavier. It said that he was carrying **the whole world and its Creator**. The child was the **infant Jesus**. The next morning, Christopher's staff is said to have blossomed.

Because he brought people safely across the river, Christopher is regarded as the **patron saint of travellers**. That is why some people have a small picture or medal of Christopher in the **car**. He is also one of the **Fourteen Holy Helpers**, a group of saints whom people asked for help in times of need. His name **Christ-bearer** fits the legend exactly.

In the Middle Ages, huge pictures of Christopher were often painted on **church walls**, usually clearly visible from outside or right by the entrance. People believed that whoever looked at Christopher was protected from a sudden death that day. There are such wall paintings in old churches in Switzerland too. In Austria, many **rescue helicopters** are now called Christophorus, each with a number.

gewusst: In pictures, Christopher is almost always shown with a child on his shoulder and a staff in his hand.
We do not know for sure whether Christopher really lived.

teile.einleitung: The wedding at Cana is a story from the Gospel of John. At a wedding feast the wine runs out, and Jesus turns water into wine.
wichtigste: The story is in the Gospel of John, chapter 2.
Cana is a place in Galilee.
Jesus, his mother Mary and his disciples are invited to the wedding.
In the middle of the feast the wine suddenly runs out.
Jesus has six stone jars filled with water, and it becomes wine.
According to John it is the first sign that Jesus performs.

abschnitte.text: In the village of **Cana** in Galilee a wedding is being celebrated. The guests include Jesus, his mother **Mary** and his disciples. Weddings then often lasted several days, and many people celebrated together. In the middle of the feast something embarrassing happens: the **wine** runs out. For the hosts this would have been a great disgrace.

Mary is the first to notice the problem and says to Jesus: “They have no more wine.” Jesus answers reservedly at first. Even so, Mary says to the servants: “**Do whatever he tells you!**” She trusts that Jesus will help. This sentence is well known to this day.

In the house stand **six stone water jars**. They were used for ritual cleansing, as was the custom among the Jews. Each jar held a great deal of water. Jesus tells the servants to fill the jars with water. The servants fill them **to the brim**. Then they are to draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.

The **master of the feast** is in charge of the food and drink at the feast. He tastes it and does not know where the wine comes from. Astonished, he tells the bridegroom that people normally serve the good wine first and the poorer wine later. This wine, however, is **better than the first**. Only the servants know what has happened.

John calls the miracles of Jesus **signs**. They are meant to show who Jesus is. According to the Gospel of John, the turning of water into wine is the **first sign**. After it his disciples believe in him. Many Christians see in the story a picture of joy and abundance: with God there is more than enough.

gewusst: The story of Cana is often read aloud in churches at wedding services.
Together the jars held several hundred litres, so a very great deal of wine for one feast.

teile.einleitung: The Prologue of John is the solemn opening of the Gospel of John. It begins with the famous words “In the beginning was the Word” and tells how God's Word became human in Jesus.
wichtigste: The Prologue covers the verses John 1:1 to 18.
The first words “In the beginning” recall the start of Genesis.
The Greek word for “word” is logos.
The verse “And the Word became flesh” is linked with the Incarnation.
In the middle of the Prologue, John the Baptist is mentioned as a witness to the light.
Goethe's Faust finally translates the opening as “In the beginning was the Deed”.

abschnitte.text: A **prologue** is an introduction. The **Prologue of John** covers the verses **John 1:1 to 18**. It begins with “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” These words recall the start of **Genesis**, the first book of the Bible: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” John wants to show by this that his story begins with creation.

In the Greek text the term for “word” is **logos**. It can also mean sense, reason or speech. The philosopher **Heraclitus** already saw in the logos an ordering law of the world. The Jewish philosopher **Philo of Alexandria** developed his own doctrine of the Logos in the 1st century. Many scholars see in this a background of the Prologue. John links the Logos with Jesus Christ.

Verse 14 says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” What is meant is that God's Word became human in **Jesus**. For this there is the term **Incarnation**, which means “becoming flesh”. The Greek verb for “dwell” really means “**to pitch a tent**”. It recalls the holy tent in which, according to the Old Testament, God lived among his people. That is why the Prologue is often read at Christmas.

In the Prologue there is often talk of the **light** that shines in the darkness. In the middle of the text **John the Baptist** is mentioned. He is not himself the light, but a **witness** to the light. In this way it becomes clear that he points to Jesus. The Prologue also speaks of the fact that not everyone receives the light.

The Prologue of John has also influenced literature. In **Goethe's Faust**, Faust tries to translate the opening of the Gospel of John. He is not satisfied with “In the beginning was the Word”. He tries “the sense” and “the power” and finally writes: “In the beginning was **the Deed**.” This scene is among the best-known passages of the drama.

gewusst: In many churches the Prologue of John is the reading on Christmas Day.
The Prologue of John is written in a very rhythmic way and is often interpreted as a hymn, that is, a song of praise.

teile.einleitung: The Way of St James is a famous pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela in Spain. Since the Middle Ages, people from all over Europe have walked there, including through Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Way of St James leads to Santiago de Compostela in the north-west of Spain.
There the tomb of the Apostle James is venerated.
The sign of the pilgrims is the scallop shell.
In the pilgrim passport, the credencial, people collect stamps.
Whoever walks at least the last 100 kilometres on foot receives a pilgrim certificate.
In 1987 the Way of St James became the first Cultural Route of the Council of Europe.

abschnitte.text: The destination of the Way of St James is the city of **Santiago de Compostela** in Galicia, in the north-west of Spain. In the great cathedral the tomb of the **Apostle James** is venerated. James was one of the twelve disciples of Jesus. According to tradition, his bones were brought to Spain and rediscovered in the 9th century. Since then people have made pilgrimages there.

The sign of the pilgrims is the **scallop shell**. Many wear it on their rucksack. The way is often marked with a yellow shell on a blue ground or with yellow arrows. On the way, pilgrims carry a passport, the **credencial**. In it they collect stamps from hostels, churches or cafés. In this way they show which route they have taken.

In Santiago you can receive a certificate, the **Compostela**, at the pilgrim office. For this you have to walk at least the last **100 kilometres** on foot. By bicycle it is at least 200 kilometres. But many pilgrims go much further, some hundreds or even thousands of kilometres. For many the way is a time for reflection, for others above all an adventure.

abschnitte.titel: Ways of St James in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Ways of St James also lead through **Switzerland**. A well-known route comes from Lake Constance and leads via **Einsiedeln** with its monastery, via Fribourg and Lausanne as far as Geneva. From there it continues through France to Spain. Pilgrims were already travelling these routes in the Middle Ages. Today the routes are well marked and used by many hikers.

In the Middle Ages, Santiago was, alongside Rome and Jerusalem, one of the most important pilgrimage destinations. The Way of St James connects many countries of Europe. That is why in **1987** it became the **first Cultural Route of the Council of Europe**. The main route through northern Spain is also part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. Since the 1980s, pilgrimage has become very popular again.

gewusst: Santiago is the Spanish form of “Saint James”.
In the cathedral of Santiago, at special services, a huge censer, the Botafumeiro, is swung through the space.

teile.einleitung: Original sin is a teaching of Christianity. It says that since the Fall of Adam, all people are affected by sin, even before they themselves do anything wrong. This teaching was shaped especially by the Church Father Augustine.
wichtigste: The Latin technical term for original sin is “peccatum originale”, sin of origin.
Augustine developed the teaching in his dispute with the monk Pelagius.
He relied especially on the Letter to the Romans, chapter 5, verse 12.
The Synod of Carthage condemned opponents of this teaching in 418.
After the Fall, Augustine called humanity the “massa damnata”.
According to Catholic teaching, original sin is removed by baptism.

abschnitte.text: The Bible tells that Adam and Eve broke God's commandment in Paradise. This is called the **Fall**. According to the teaching of **original sin**, this act has consequences for all people. The Latin term for it is **peccatum originale**, that is, “sin of origin”. This is distinguished from a person's own personal deeds, the **actual sins**.

The monk **Pelagius** stressed that people can do good by their own strength. He denied that Adam's sin had corrupted the nature of all people. The Church Father **Augustine** contradicted him in many writings. For him, all people needed the **grace of God** in order to be saved. He called humanity since Adam a **“massa damnata”**, a condemned mass.

Augustine relied especially on the **Letter to the Romans**, chapter 5, verse 12. In the Latin version he read “in quo omnes peccaverunt”, in him, that is, in Adam, all have sinned. The **Greek text** is, however, ambiguous at this point. That is why not all experts understand it in the same way. Even so, Augustine's interpretation became very influential in the West.

In the year **418** the **Synod of Carthage** condemned the opponents of Augustine's teaching. Pope Zosimus agreed with this. Much later, in 1546, the **Council of Trent** affirmed that **baptism** takes away the guilt of original sin. With this it also confirmed the baptism of small children.

Not all churches understand original sin in the same way. The **Orthodox churches** speak more of the consequences of the Fall, such as mortality, than of guilt. The **Reformers**, such as Luther and Calvin, even stressed original sin particularly strongly. Today many theologians interpret the teaching to mean that all people are born into a world in which evil exists.

gewusst: Augustine lived in North Africa and was bishop of the city of Hippo in what is now Algeria.
Judaism has no teaching of original sin in the Christian sense.

teile.einleitung: All Saints' Day is a Christian festival on 1 November. On this day the Church celebrates all the saints together. Many families then visit the cemetery and decorate the graves of their dead.
wichtigste: All Saints' Day is on 1 November every year.
On this day people remember all the saints together.
Saints are seen as role models in faith.
Many families visit the cemetery and put candles on the graves.
On 2 November All Souls' Day follows.
Halloween is the evening before All Saints' Day.
In Catholic cantons All Saints' Day is usually a public holiday.

abschnitte.text: **Saints** are people who believed very firmly in God and did a lot of good. The Church honours them as **role models** in faith. There are very many saints. Many have a feast day of their own in the year, but by no means all. That is why on **All Saints' Day** people remember all the saints together, including those whom nobody knows by name.

All Saints' Day is on **1 November** every year. It is mainly a **Catholic** festival. The day after, on 2 November, is **All Souls' Day**. Then people pray for all the dead. The two days belong closely together. Many people already use All Saints' Day to visit the grave, because in some regions it is a day off.

On All Saints' Day many families go to the **cemetery**. They visit the graves of dead relatives, think of them and pray. Beforehand the graves are made to look nice. People bring **flowers**, arrangements and wreaths. **Grave lights** are placed on the graves. The light is a sign of **hope**.

The word **Halloween** comes from the English “All Hallows' Eve”. That means the **evening before All Saints' Day**. So Halloween is celebrated on 31 October. The custom with pumpkins and costumes comes from Ireland and the USA. In recent decades it has become popular in Switzerland too.

In Switzerland the **cantons** decide on many public holidays. All Saints' Day is a public holiday mainly in cantons with a **Catholic** tradition, for example **Lucerne** or **Valais**. In cantons with a Reformed tradition such as Zurich or Bern, 1 November is an ordinary working day. On 31 October, by contrast, many Reformed people celebrate Reformation Day.

gewusst: In the Catholic Church, All Saints' Day has been celebrated on 1 November since the 9th century.
The Orthodox churches celebrate a festival of all the saints on the first Sunday after Pentecost.

teile.einleitung: Liberation theology is a Christian movement that arose above all in Latin America. It asks what faith means for poor and oppressed people. Within the Catholic Church it was controversial for a long time.
wichtigste: Liberation theology arose in the 1960s and 1970s in Latin America.
The assembly of bishops at Medellín in 1968 made poverty a central theme.
Its guiding concept is the “preferential option for the poor”.
In base communities, lay people read the Bible together.
It often works by the three steps “see, judge, act”.
In 1984 the Vatican criticised the adoption of Marxist analysis of society.

abschnitte.text: In Latin America many people lived in great poverty, while a few were very rich. Many priests and theologians asked what the Gospel means in this situation. In **1968** the Latin American bishops met in **Medellín** in Colombia. There **poverty and oppression** became central themes of the Church. The Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez gave the movement its name with a book.

The guiding concept is the **preferential option for the poor**. That means: the Church should first take the side of the poor, as Jesus did. Faith should not only be a comfort for the next world, but improve life already today. The theologians often work by the three steps **see, judge, act**: look at the situation, judge it in the light of the Bible and then do something.

In small groups, the **base communities**, lay people came together, that is, believers without the office of priest. They read the Bible together and talked about their own situation in life. Many also learned to read and write in this way. The Nicaraguan priest and poet **Ernesto Cardenal** founded one such community. In 1979 he became **Minister of Culture** in the Sandinista government.

The Vatican viewed the movement critically. In **1984** the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith criticised in particular the **adoption of Marxist analysis of society**. In 1985 Rome imposed a **penitential silence** on the Brazilian theologian **Leonardo Boff**: for a time he was not allowed to teach in public. Other parts of the movement, such as concern for the poor, the Church did adopt.

Some representatives of the movement paid for their commitment with their lives. Archbishop **Óscar Romero** of San Salvador was killed in 1980 during a service. In 1989 the Jesuit **Ignacio Ellacuría**, rector of the Central American University, was murdered with fellow Jesuits. Romero was canonised in 2018.

gewusst: The three steps “see, judge, act” originally come from the Catholic Working Youth in Belgium.
In Switzerland too, church aid agencies still support projects in Latin America today.

teile.einleitung: The Baptists are a Protestant free church. Their name comes from the Greek word for “to baptise”. It is typical that they baptise only people who themselves believe in Jesus Christ.
wichtigste: Baptists baptise only people who themselves believe.
Baptism is usually by immersion.
John Smyth founded the first Baptist congregation in Amsterdam in 1609.
Each congregation decides its own affairs.
Most Baptists live in the USA.
The worldwide union is called the Baptist World Alliance.

abschnitte.text: Baptists do not baptise infants. In their conviction, a person should decide for the faith **themselves** and then be baptised. This is called **believers' baptism**. Usually the whole body is briefly **immersed**, as described in the Bible for baptism in the Jordan. For this, many Baptist churches have a baptismal pool of their own.

The Baptists arose in the 17th century from English Protestants who were persecuted in their homeland. Some fled to the Netherlands. There **John Smyth** founded the first Baptist congregation in **Amsterdam** in **1609**. Soon congregations arose in England too. From there the movement spread to North America and across the world.

Among the Baptists there are no bishops who decide over the congregations. Each **congregation decides its own affairs**, for example whom it elects as pastor. **Religious freedom** and the separation of church and state are also important to Baptists. Many congregations work together in unions. Worldwide they are linked in the **Baptist World Alliance**.

Most Baptists in the world live in the **USA**. There they are among the largest churches of all. The civil rights leader **Martin Luther King** was pastor of a Baptist church. He fought non-violently for equal rights for Black and white people. The evangelist **Billy Graham**, who preached before millions of people worldwide, was also a Baptist.

gewusst: There are Baptist congregations in Switzerland too, joined together in a union of their own.
Many well-known gospel songs come from African American Baptist churches in the USA.

teile.einleitung: HEKS is the **aid organisation of the Protestant Reformed Church of Switzerland**. It was founded in **1946** and helps people in need, abroad and in Switzerland. In French-speaking Switzerland it is called **EPER**.
wichtigste: HEKS was founded in 1946 by the Reformed churches.
At first it helped people in war-torn Europe.
Its head office is in Zurich.
In French it is called EPER.
In 2021 it merged with Brot für alle (Bread for All).
With Fastenaktion (Lent Campaign) it runs the Ecumenical Campaign.

abschnitte.text: After the **Second World War**, many cities in Europe lay in ruins. The Reformed churches of Switzerland founded HEKS in **1946** to help the people there. It brought emergency aid such as food, clothes and help with rebuilding. Later, projects in Africa, Asia and Latin America were added. Today HEKS is one of the large aid organisations of Switzerland.

The **head office** of HEKS is in **Zurich**. There are also regional offices in various cantons. In French-speaking Switzerland the aid organisation is called **Entraide Protestante Suisse**, abbreviated **EPER**. But it is the same organisation. In November 2021 the merger with the aid organisation **Brot für alle** (Bread for All) became legally valid.

HEKS works in many countries of the world. An important theme is the **right to land and food**. Small farmers should be able to keep their land and grow enough to eat. Other focuses are flight and migration as well as climate justice. After disasters HEKS also provides **emergency aid**.

In Switzerland too, HEKS stands up for disadvantaged people. For example, it offers **legal advice for asylum seekers**. There are also projects that help people with integration. Together with the Catholic aid organisation **Fastenaktion** (Lent Campaign), HEKS runs the **Ecumenical Campaign** in the period before Easter. The sale of roses is well known in this campaign.

gewusst: Ecumenical means that different Christian churches work together.
Brot für alle was known above all for its campaign during Lent.

teile.einleitung: The Evangelical Reformed Church came into being in the Reformation of the 16th century. In Switzerland, Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich and John Calvin in Geneva shaped this church. Today it is one of the great national churches of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Reformed church arose in the Reformation in Zurich and Geneva.
Bern introduced the Reformation in 1528 after the Bern Disputation.
The Zurich Bible was printed in full in 1531.
Zwingli died in 1531 at the Battle of Kappel.
The Reformed church has two sacraments: baptism and the Lord's Supper.
Since 2020 the national association has been called the Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: From 1519, **Huldrych Zwingli** preached at the Grossmünster in Zurich. He wanted to renew the Church according to the Bible. Other cities followed. **Bern** introduced the Reformation in 1528 after a great religious debate, the **Bern Disputation**. In Geneva, **John Calvin** worked later. Zwingli died in 1531 at the **Battle of Kappel** in the war against Catholic cantons.

For the Reformed, the **Bible** is the most important foundation of faith. That is why everyone should be able to read it in their own language. The **Zurich Bible** was printed in full in 1531. It is still revised and used today. In the service the sermon is at the centre.

Reformed churches are usually plain. In the Reformation, **pictures and statues were removed**. The Reformers felt that they distract from the Word of God. Instead of an altar there is often a simple communion table at the front. The Reformed church knows only two **sacraments**: **baptism** and the **Lord's Supper**.

In Geneva, the **Reformation Wall** stands in the Parc des Bastions. It is a long wall with large stone figures. In the middle stand Calvin and other Reformers from Geneva. It was begun in 1909 for the 400th anniversary of Calvin's birth.

In Switzerland the Reformed church is organised independently in each canton. Many are state-recognised **national churches**. Since 2020 the national association has been called the **Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland**. The congregations often choose their pastors themselves, and both women and men can hold the office.

gewusst: In 1522, people in Zurich publicly ate sausages during Lent. Zwingli defended them, and this triggered a great dispute.
The Reformation Wall in Geneva is about 100 metres long.

t1dpjpqz.t: The twelve-year-old Jesus in the Temple

teile.einleitung: The story of the twelve-year-old Jesus in the Temple is found in the Gospel of Luke. Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem after a festival, and his parents search for him for three days. It is the only story in the Gospels from the youth of Jesus.
wichtigste: Jesus was twelve years old when he travelled to Jerusalem with his parents.
The family made a pilgrimage every year for the festival of Passover.
Only after a day's journey did Mary and Joseph notice that Jesus was missing.
After three days they found him in the Temple with the teachers.
Everyone was amazed at his understanding and his answers.
Jesus called the Temple his Father's house.
After that he returned to Nazareth with his parents.

abschnitte.titel: The journey to the Passover festival
abschnitte.text: The family of Jesus lived in **Nazareth**. Every year they travelled to **Jerusalem** for the Jewish festival of **Passover**. This festival recalls the liberation from Egypt. When Jesus was **twelve years** old, he went along again. After the festival, Mary and Joseph set off for home with many other travellers.

Mary and Joseph thought that Jesus was with relatives or acquaintances in the travelling group. Only **after a day's journey** did they notice that he was missing. They searched for him everywhere and returned to Jerusalem. Only **after three days** did they finally find him. He was in the **Temple**.

abschnitte.titel: In the midst of the teachers
abschnitte.text: Jesus was sitting among the **teachers** in the Temple. He listened to them and asked them questions. Everyone who heard him was **amazed** at his understanding and his answers. His mother said they had been looking for him full of worry. Jesus answered, in essence: “Did you not know that I must be in my **Father's house**?” By the Father he meant God.

His parents did not understand what Jesus meant by this. But he went back with them to **Nazareth** and obeyed them. Mary **kept all these things in her heart**, which means she thought about them for a long time. The Gospel of Luke goes on to say that Jesus grew in wisdom and in years. About the following years until his work as an adult, the Gospels say nothing.

Many artists have painted the scene. Often you see a young Jesus between older, bearded scholars. Albrecht Dürer painted a picture of it in 1506. The painter Max Liebermann also showed the scene in 1879. His picture caused fierce discussion at the time, because he showed Jesus as a perfectly ordinary boy.

gewusst: From Nazareth to Jerusalem it is over 100 kilometres, and families usually went on foot.
In art the scene is also called “Jesus among the scribes”.

teile.einleitung: In the first centuries after Christ, Christians in the Roman Empire were persecuted again and again. Some persecutions affected only one city, others the whole empire. Only in the 4th century were Christians allowed to practise their faith freely.
wichtigste: After the great fire of Rome in the year 64, Emperor Nero blamed the Christians.
The historian Tacitus reports on this in his Annals.
Christians refused to make sacrifices to the emperor as a divine ruler.
Around 250, Emperor Decius ordered the first persecution across the whole empire.
In the year 303, the last and greatest persecution began under Diocletian.
The Greek word “martyr” means “witness”.
In Switzerland, Saint-Maurice, Zurich and Solothurn recall martyrs from legend.

abschnitte.titel: Nero and the fire of Rome
abschnitte.text: In the year 64, a large part of the city of Rome burned down. Many people believed that Emperor Nero was to blame himself. To divert attention from these rumours, he accused the Christians. The Roman historian **Tacitus** reports in his **Annals** how Nero had them harshly punished. Tacitus was not a Christian himself, which is why his account is an important source.

In the Roman Empire there were many gods, and foreign religions were usually tolerated. But the **imperial cult** included making sacrifices to the emperor as if he were a god. Christians refused, because they worshipped only one God. So some people saw them as enemies of the state. For a long time there was no persecution everywhere, only individual cases in certain regions.

Around the year 250, Emperor **Decius** demanded that all inhabitants of the empire sacrifice to the gods. Those who did so received a certificate. Those who refused were punished. In the year 303, the greatest persecution began under Emperor **Diocletian**. Churches were destroyed and holy books burned, and many Christians were put in prison or killed.

In the year 311, Emperor Galerius issued an edict of toleration that ended the persecution. In 313 the emperors **Constantine** and Licinius agreed in Milan that all religions could be practised freely. Later, Christianity even became the most important religion of the empire. People who had died for their faith were honoured as **martyrs**, that is, as witnesses of their faith.

According to legend, the **Theban Legion** and its leader **Maurice** were executed at Agaunum because the soldiers refused to kill Christians or to sacrifice to the gods. The place is now called **Saint-Maurice** in the canton of Valais. In Zurich, **Felix and Regula** are regarded as the patron saints of the city, and they can still be seen on the city seal today. In Solothurn, **Ursus and Victor** are honoured, and the St Ursus Cathedral is dedicated to them.

gewusst: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice in Valais was founded in the year 515 and is regarded as one of the oldest surviving monasteries in the West.
Tacitus is one of the first non-Christian writers to mention Christ.

teile.einleitung: Isaiah is one of the great prophets of the Old Testament. He worked in Jerusalem, and the book named after him is among the most important books of the Bible for Jews and Christians.
wichtigste: Isaiah appeared in the 8th century BC.
He worked in Jerusalem in the kingdom of Judah.
The Book of Isaiah has 66 chapters.
The picture of peace “swords into ploughshares” comes from it.
