At Qumran by the Dead Sea an almost complete Isaiah scroll over 2,000 years old was found.

abschnitte.text: Isaiah lived in the **8th century BC** and worked in **Jerusalem**. At that time the mighty Assyrian Empire threatened the small kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Isaiah advised and admonished the kings. He called on them to trust in God instead of in alliances with foreign powers. He also criticised the rich when they exploited the poor. Many scholars think that the later chapters of the book come from other authors who wrote in his tradition.

In the Book of Isaiah there is a famous vision of peace: the nations will beat their **swords into ploughshares** and no longer learn to make war. A ploughshare is the iron blade of the plough with which the soil is broken up. This image became the motto of many **peace movements**, for example in East Germany in the 1980s. Christians also read many passages from Isaiah at Christmas, because they see in them pointers to Jesus.

In 1947 shepherds found old scrolls in caves near **Qumran** by the **Dead Sea**. Among them was an almost complete scroll of the Book of **Isaiah**. It is **over 2,000 years old** and thus much older than most other known manuscripts of the Bible. It is astonishing that its text is very similar to the text handed down later. Today it is kept in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

gewusst: The great Isaiah scroll from Qumran is over 7 metres long.
The name Isaiah means roughly “God is salvation”.

teile.einleitung: The story of Daniel in the lions' den is found in the Book of Daniel in the Old Testament. Despite a ban, Daniel went on praying to God and was thrown to the lions for it. The next morning he was unharmed.
wichtigste: As a young man Daniel was taken away from Jerusalem to Babylon.
At the king's court he became a high official.
Jealous officials wanted to harm him and brought about a law against praying to God.
Daniel went on praying three times a day, with his windows open towards Jerusalem.
King Darius had to have him thrown into the lions' den, which was closed with a stone.
The king could not sleep all night.
In the morning Daniel said that an angel had shut the lions' mouths.

abschnitte.text: The king of **Babylon** conquered Jerusalem and brought young men to his capital. One of them was **Daniel**. He was clever and reliable. That is why King **Darius** later made him one of his chief **officials**. The king liked Daniel very much and wanted to give him even more responsibility.

Other officials were **jealous** of Daniel. They looked for a reason to accuse him but could find no fault. So they persuaded the king to pass a law: for 30 days no one was allowed to pray to any god or man except the king. Anyone who did so anyway was to be thrown into the **lions' den**. A law like that could no longer be changed.

Daniel knew about the ban. Even so, he prayed to God **three times a day** as always. He opened the windows of his room towards **Jerusalem**, his homeland. The jealous officials watched him and denounced him to the king. Darius was sad but had to keep to his own law.

Daniel was thrown into the den, and a large **stone** was laid over the opening. The king sealed it with his ring. During the night Darius ate nothing and **could not sleep**. Early in the morning he hurried to the den and called out to Daniel. Daniel answered that God had sent his **angel**, who had shut the lions' mouths. He was unharmed.

The king was overjoyed and had Daniel brought out. Then he ordered that everyone in the kingdom should respect the God of Daniel. The story tells of **courage** and **trust**: Daniel stayed true to his faith even when it became dangerous. It is still told in children's Bibles today and has often been painted.

gewusst: The same book also contains the story of three friends of Daniel who were kept safe in a fiery furnace.
Babylon lay in the area of present-day Iraq.

teile.einleitung: The Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland, EKS for short, is the union of the Reformed churches of Switzerland. It represents the Reformed at national level. Until the end of 2019 it was called the Swiss Protestant Church Federation.
wichtigste: Until the end of 2019 the EKS was called the Swiss Protestant Church Federation.
The Church Federation was founded in Olten in 1920.
The EKS has its seat in Bern.
Its parliament is called the Synod and meets twice a year.
The Council has seven members.
Rita Famos was elected the first woman president in 2020.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Protestant Church Federation** was founded in **1920** in **Olten**. It united the Reformed churches of the cantons. Since 1 January 2020 it has been called the **Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland**. With the new name, people wanted to show that the Reformed are one church at national level too. Its seat is in **Bern**.

The parliament of the EKS is called the **Synod**. It meets **twice a year**. The delegates come from the member churches. The executive is the **Council** with **seven** members. It leads the church between meetings of the Synod. In 2021 the EKS had **25** member churches.

In 2020 the Synod elected **Rita Famos** president of the Council. She was the first woman in this office. She is a pastor and took up the office in 2021. The president often represents the Reformed in public.

In 1946 the Church Federation founded the aid organisation **HEKS**. It helps people in Switzerland and in other countries. In 1973 the Church Federation, the Catholic Bishops' Conference and the Christ Catholic Church jointly declared **mutual recognition of baptism**. Anyone baptised in one of these churches does not have to be baptised again when changing church.

gewusst: HEKS was founded after the Second World War to help with rebuilding in Europe.
The Evangelical Methodist Church is also one of the member churches of the EKS.

teile.einleitung: The First Vatican Council was a great assembly of Catholic bishops in Rome. It met in 1869 and 1870. Its best-known decision is the one on the infallibility of the Pope.
wichtigste: Pope Pius IX summoned the council.
It met from 1869 to 1870 in the Vatican.
The constitution “Pastor aeternus” laid down the infallibility of the Pope.
The vote on 18 July 1870 ended with 533 to 2.
“Dei Filius” dealt with faith and reason.
The council did not end in the normal way, because Italian troops took Rome.

abschnitte.text: Pope **Pius IX** summoned the council. It began in December 1869 in St Peter's Basilica. Hundreds of bishops from all over the world travelled to Rome. The Church wanted to respond to the new ideas of the time, for example to the belief that only reason and science count.

The constitution **“Dei Filius”** deals mainly with the relationship between **faith and reason**. It teaches that God can also be known through reason. According to this teaching, faith and reason should not contradict each other. A constitution is an important teaching document of a council.

In the constitution **“Pastor aeternus”**, the **infallibility** of the Pope was laid down as a dogma in 1870. A dogma is a binding statement of belief. The Pope is infallible only when he speaks **ex cathedra**, that is, when he decides solemnly as supreme teacher on matters of faith or morals. In the vote on 18 July 1870, 533 council fathers voted for it and 2 against. Many opponents had left beforehand.

Shortly after the vote, war broke out between France and Germany. The French troops that protected Rome withdrew. In September 1870 **Italian troops** took Rome. The Papal States came to an end, and the Pope suspended the council. It was never formally concluded.

Not all Catholics accepted the dogma. The Munich theologian **Ignaz von Döllinger** rejected it and was excommunicated in 1871, that is, expelled from the Church. From the resistance the **Old Catholics** arose. In Switzerland this church is called the **Christ Catholic Church**.

gewusst: Only almost 100 years later, with the Second Vatican Council from 1962, did a council meet in the Vatican again.
Pius IX was Pope for over 31 years, longer than anyone else after Peter.

teile.einleitung: A free church is a Christian church that is independent of the state. Members join deliberately and fund their church themselves. In Switzerland there are many different free churches.
wichtigste: Free churches are independent of the state.
People usually become members deliberately and pay no church tax.
The Mennonites go back to the Anabaptist movement, which arose in Zurich around 1525.
The Seventh-day Adventists hold their service on Saturday.
William Booth founded the Salvation Army in London in 1865.
The Chrischona movement has its centre on St Chrischona near Basel.
The free church ICF was founded in Zurich in 1996.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, the Reformed and Catholic churches are **national churches** (Landeskirchen) in most cantons. They are recognised by the state, and their members often pay church tax. A **free church**, by contrast, is **independent of the state**. It is funded by donations from its members. People usually become members deliberately, often as teenagers or adults.

One of the oldest free churches goes back to the **Anabaptist movement**. It arose around **1525** in **Zurich**. The Anabaptists baptised only people who believe for themselves, and for this they were persecuted for a long time. From them came the **Mennonites**. They are named after Menno Simons, a leader of the Anabaptists in the Netherlands.

In **1865**, **William Booth** founded a movement in London from which the **Salvation Army** developed. It helps the poor, the homeless and people in need, and links this with faith. The Salvation Army is organised like an army. Its leaders are called **officers**, and many wear uniform. In Switzerland it is also known for its Christmas kettles in the towns and cities.

The **Seventh-day Adventists** hold their weekly service on **Saturday**. They keep the commandment of the Bible to keep the seventh day holy as a day of rest. The name “Adventists” comes from the fact that they expect the early return of Christ. Many of them also pay particular attention to a healthy way of life.

On the hill of **St Chrischona** near Basel lies the well-known centre of the **Chrischona movement**. There, people have been trained for church service since the 19th century. The free church **ICF** was founded in **Zurich** in **1996**. It is known for modern music and services with a lot of technology and now has congregations in several countries.

gewusst: The Mennonites and the Amish have their roots partly in the canton of Bern, for example in the Emmental.
The television tower on St Chrischona is the tallest free-standing structure in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Printing with movable type was invented around 1450 by Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. It helped the Reformation greatly, because writings could now be spread quickly and cheaply. Martin Luther became the most printed author of his time.
wichtigste: Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type around 1450.
Through printing, ideas spread quickly and cheaply.
Pamphlets were short printed booklets on one subject.
Luther was the most printed author of his time.
Luther's complete translation of the Bible appeared in 1534.
Christoph Froschauer printed the Zurich Bible in Zurich in 1531.

abschnitte.text: In the past, books had to be copied laboriously by hand. That took a long time and was expensive. Around **1450**, **Johannes Gutenberg** in **Mainz** invented printing with **movable type** made of metal. With it, many identical pages could be produced in a short time. Books became much cheaper and more numerous.

At the time of the Reformation, many **pamphlets** were printed. These were **short printed booklets** on a particular subject. They were cheap and could be spread quickly. In this way many people learned of the new ideas. **Ideas spread quickly and cheaply**, even over great distances.

**Martin Luther** wrote very many writings in German so that everyone could understand them. In **1520** he published **“On the Freedom of a Christian”**. He was the **most printed author** of his time. His complete **translation of the Bible** appeared in **1534**. It had a great influence on the German language.

Many people could not read at that time. That is why **pictures** were very important. The painter **Lucas Cranach the Elder** was a friend of Luther. He created many **woodcuts** and portraits for his writings. Woodcuts could be printed together with the text. Portraits of Luther also became widely known in this way.

In Switzerland too, printing played a great role. In **Zurich** the printer **Christoph Froschauer** worked closely with Zwingli. In **1531** he printed the complete **Zurich Bible** in German, with many pictures. It appeared even before Luther's complete Bible. Basel too was an important city of printing at that time.

gewusst: Of the Gutenberg Bible, around 49 copies survive worldwide, complete or in part.
The Zurich Bible is still revised today, and a new version appeared in 2007.

teile.einleitung: The German Peasants' War was a great uprising of peasants and ordinary people in the years 1524 to 1526. They demanded more rights and fewer payments, and in doing so they appealed to the Bible. The princes crushed the uprising bloodily.
wichtigste: In 1525 the “Twelve Articles” with the peasants' demands were written in Memmingen.
The first article demanded that every community may choose its own pastor.
The peasants demanded an end to serfdom, because Christ had redeemed all people.
On 15 May 1525 the army around Thomas Müntzer was defeated at Frankenhausen.
In a sharp pamphlet, Luther called on the princes to act harshly.
The Swabian League under Georg Truchsess von Waldburg defeated the peasants in southern Germany.
About 70,000 to 75,000 people lost their lives.

abschnitte.text: At that time many peasants lived in great dependence on their lords. They had to pay **dues** and perform services. Some were **serfs**, which means they belonged to a lord and were not free to move away. Through the **Reformation**, many people read and heard the Bible in a new way. They felt that according to God's word, all people ought to be treated more fairly.

In 1525 the furrier **Sebastian Lotzer** and the preacher **Christoph Schappeler** wrote the **Twelve Articles** in the imperial city of **Memmingen**. The first article demanded that every community may **choose its own pastor**. The third demanded the end of serfdom, because Christ had redeemed all people, the shepherd as well as the highest. The articles were printed very many times in a short space of time.

The peasants gathered in large groups called **bands** (Haufen). But they were poorly equipped. In southern Germany the **Swabian League** defeated the peasant bands. Its commander Georg Truchsess von Waldburg was given the nickname “Bauernjörg” (Peasant George). On 15 May 1525, at the **Battle of Frankenhausen** in Thuringia, the army around the preacher **Thomas Müntzer** was defeated. Müntzer was executed shortly afterwards.

The peasants had hoped for **Martin Luther**. But Luther felt that the rebels were wrongly appealing to the Gospel. In his pamphlet **“Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants”** he called on the princes to act harshly against the rebels. This pamphlet damaged his reputation among many ordinary people.

In the Peasants' War an estimated **70,000 to 75,000** people lost their lives, mostly rebels. Many survivors were also burdened with punishments and dues. The preacher Christoph Schappeler came from **St Gallen** and fled back there after the war. The demands of the Twelve Articles are regarded today as an early example of the call for rights and freedoms.

gewusst: The Twelve Articles were printed in about 25,000 copies within a few months.
In Switzerland, too, there was a great peasants' war in 1653, but it had other causes.

teile.einleitung: First Communion is a great festival in the Catholic Church. Children receive the host for the first time. In Switzerland they are usually in the 3rd class at school.
wichtigste: First Communion is celebrated in the Catholic Church.
The children receive the host for the first time.
A host is a thin, round piece of bread.
“Communion” means fellowship.
Communion recalls the last meal of Jesus.
The children often wear white clothes and hold a candle.

abschnitte.text: In the Catholic Mass, believers receive the **host**. This is a thin, round bread made of flour and water. For Catholics, Jesus Christ himself is present in it. The word **Communion** comes from Latin and means **fellowship**. What is meant is fellowship with Jesus and with the other people in the Church.

Communion recalls the evening before the death of Jesus. At that time he ate a **last meal** with his disciples. He broke the bread and shared it with them. In doing so he asked them to do this in remembrance of him. Ever since then Christians have celebrated this meal again and again.

In Switzerland children usually celebrate First Communion in the **3rd class**. Before that they attend religious education. There they learn stories of Jesus, prayers and the order of the Mass. Often meetings in the parish are also part of it, where the children make crafts and sing.

The children often wear **white** clothes or a white robe. White recalls baptism. Many hold a **candle** in their hand. After the service the families celebrate together with relatives and godparents. In the past First Communion was often on **White Sunday**, the Sunday after Easter. Today many parishes celebrate on another Sunday in spring.

gewusst: White Sunday is so called because in the early Church, the newly baptised wore their white baptismal robes for the last time on that day.
In Protestant churches there is no First Communion; there they celebrate the Lord's Supper.

teile.einleitung: Love of enemies means loving even those who do evil to you. Jesus demands it in the Sermon on the Mount. It is one of the best-known and most difficult commandments of Christianity.
wichtigste: Jesus says in Matthew 5:44: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.”
In doing so he takes up the old rule “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth”.
Instead of hitting back, you should also turn the other cheek.
On the cross Jesus asks: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”
Stephen, as he was dying, prayed for the people who were killing him.

abschnitte.titel: The commandment in the Sermon on the Mount
abschnitte.text: In the **Sermon on the Mount** in the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” This is in **Matthew 5:44**. It does not mean that you have to approve of everything others do. But you should not meet them with hatred, but wish them well. Jesus explains this by saying that God makes the sun rise on the good and the evil.

In the Old Testament there is the rule **“an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth”**. It was meant to prevent the punishment from being greater than the harm. Jesus goes beyond this. He says that if someone strikes you on the right cheek, you should turn the **other cheek** as well. With this he wants to show that violence should not be passed on.

According to the Gospel of Luke, Jesus prays on the cross for the people who crucify him: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” According to the Acts of the Apostles, **Stephen**, the first Christian **martyr**, also prayed for his killers as he was dying. A martyr is a person who dies for their faith. Later, people such as Martin Luther King also appealed to love of enemies when they worked for justice without violence.

gewusst: The commandment of love of enemies is also found in the Gospel of Luke, in the so-called Sermon on the Plain.

teile.einleitung: The Acts of the Apostles is a book in the New Testament. It tells how the first Christian congregations formed after Jesus' ascension. At its centre are the apostles Peter and Paul.
wichtigste: The Acts of the Apostles begins with the ascension of Jesus.
It tells of the first congregation in Jerusalem.
Seven men were chosen as helpers to look after the widows.
The Roman centurion Cornelius was one of the first non-Jews to be baptised.
An angel freed Peter from prison.
On the way to Rome, Paul was shipwrecked off Malta.
The book ends with Paul preaching on in Rome under guard.

abschnitte.text: The **Acts of the Apostles** is the fifth book of the New Testament. It is regarded as a continuation of the **Gospel of Luke** and is ascribed to the same author. In the first chapter Jesus is taken up into heaven before the eyes of the disciples. This is called the **Ascension**. After that begins the story of the first Christian **congregation** in Jerusalem.

The first Christians in **Jerusalem** shared their property with one another. The apostles wanted to concentrate on prayer and preaching. So the congregation chose **seven men** as helpers to look after the **widows**. In this people see the beginning of the **office of deacon**. The Acts of the Apostles also tells of **Ananias and Sapphira**. The couple secretly kept back money from the sale of a field and lied about it. The story warns against dishonesty.

In the first part of the book Peter is the most important person. He visited the Roman **centurion Cornelius** in **Caesarea** and baptised him with his family. Cornelius was one of the first **non-Jews** to become Christians. In this way the congregation opened itself to all people. Later King **Herod Agrippa** had Peter locked up. According to the Acts of the Apostles, an **angel** loosed his chains at night and led him out.

In the second part **Paul** is at the centre. He travelled through many countries around the Mediterranean and founded congregations. In the end he was arrested and taken as a prisoner to **Rome**. On the way the ship was wrecked in a storm off the island of **Malta**. But everyone reached the shore. A bay on Malta is still named after Paul today.

In the last chapter Paul lives for **two years** in a rented flat in Rome. He is guarded, but may receive visitors and **goes on preaching**. With this the book ends. The Acts of the Apostles says nothing about the death of Paul. Many scholars see in this a sign that the message goes on, “to the ends of the earth”.

gewusst: The Acts of the Apostles is the only book in the New Testament that tells the time of the first congregations as a connected story.
In the Acts of the Apostles, the followers of Jesus are called “Christians” for the first time in Antioch.

teile.einleitung: The Walk to Canossa is a famous event from the Middle Ages. In January **1077**, King Henry IV went as a penitent to Pope Gregory VII in order to be freed from excommunication. To this day people say “to go to Canossa” when someone has to humble themselves and ask for forgiveness.
wichtigste: Henry IV went to Canossa in the year 1077.
Pope Gregory VII was staying in the castle of Matilda of Tuscany.
Henry is said to have waited three days in a penitent's robe in front of the castle.
After that the Pope lifted the excommunication.
The background was the Investiture Controversy between emperor and Pope.
Otto von Bismarck said in 1872: “We shall not go to Canossa.”

abschnitte.text: In the 11th century the king and the Pope quarrelled over who might appoint bishops. This dispute is called the **Investiture Controversy**. Henry IV wanted to have Pope Gregory VII deposed. In 1076 the Pope answered with **excommunication**: Henry was expelled from the Church. Many princes now threatened to stop recognising Henry as king.

Canossa is a castle in northern Italy that belonged to the powerful **Matilda of Tuscany**. Pope Gregory VII had withdrawn there. In the middle of winter, Henry crossed the Alps to meet the Pope. He was determined to be freed from the ban before the princes decided against him.

According to the sources, Henry waited **three days** in a simple penitent's robe in front of the castle gate. He asked the Pope for forgiveness. Matilda and Abbot Hugh of Cluny spoke up for him. In the end Gregory VII lifted the ban. With this Henry had saved his position as king for the time being.

The Walk to Canossa became an image for **humiliation**. In the 19th century the state in Germany quarrelled with the Catholic Church; this dispute is called the **Kulturkampf**. In 1872 Reich Chancellor **Otto von Bismarck** said in the Reichstag: “We shall not go to Canossa.” He meant that he would not bow to the Church.

gewusst: Historians still argue today whether Canossa was more of a defeat or a clever move by Henry.
Today only ruins are left of Canossa Castle.

teile.einleitung: David and Goliath is one of the best-known stories in the Bible. It tells how the youngest son of a shepherd family defeats the giant warrior Goliath. David had courage because he trusted in God.
wichtigste: David was the youngest son of his father.
He brought food to his older brothers in the army camp.
Goliath challenged the Israelites to a fight for 40 days.
Goliath wore a bronze helmet and heavy armour.
As a shepherd, David had already defeated lions and bears.
David's stone hit Goliath on the forehead, and then the Philistines fled.
David's best friend was Jonathan, the king's son.

abschnitte.text: **David** was the **youngest** of several brothers. He lived in Bethlehem and looked after his father's sheep. His older brothers were **soldiers** in King Saul's army. One day his father sent David to them in the camp with **bread and cheese**. There David heard the giant Goliath mocking the Israelites.

**Goliath** was the strongest warrior of the **Philistines**. He wore a **bronze helmet** and heavy armour. For **40 days**, every morning and evening, he stepped forward and challenged the Israelites. No one in Israel dared to fight him. All the soldiers were afraid of him.

David told King Saul that he wanted to fight Goliath. Saul thought David was far too young. But David told him that he had already rescued his sheep from **lions and bears**. He said that God had protected him then and would protect him now too. David trusted completely in **God**.

David walked towards Goliath with his sling and a few stones. He shouted that he came **in the name of God**. Then he slung a stone. It hit Goliath on the **forehead**, and the giant fell over. When the Philistines saw that their strongest fighter was dead, they **fled**. The Israelites pursued them.

After the victory David came to the court of King Saul. There he met **Jonathan**, the king's son. The two were very fond of each other and became **close friends**. Jonathan even gave David his cloak and his weapons. Their friendship is still seen today as an example of great loyalty.

gewusst: According to the Bible, Goliath came from the city of Gath.
The story is in the First Book of Samuel in the Old Testament.

t1k0stno.t: Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer

teile.einleitung: The Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer (Bettag) is a holiday in Switzerland. In most cantons it falls on the third Sunday in September. It is not a purely church holiday but a state holiday that is meant to unite all denominations.
wichtigste: In most cantons the Bettag is on the third Sunday in September.
The Federal Diet fixed this date in 1832.
Geneva celebrates its own day of prayer, the Jeûne genevois, on a Thursday.
In Vaud the Monday after the Bettag is a public holiday.
With Bettag proclamations, the authorities called people to the Bettag.
As state secretary of Zurich, Gottfried Keller wrote Bettag proclamations.
Since the Second Vatican Council the Bettag has been celebrated ecumenically in many places.

abschnitte.text: In the past, the individual places of the Confederation ordered days of prayer, for example in times of need. Catholic and Reformed places celebrated on different days. On 17 September **1797** both denominations held a day of prayer **together** for the first time. In 1798 the **Helvetic Republic** issued a proclamation for the whole country for the first time. In 1832 the **Federal Diet** fixed the third Sunday in September.

The name says what it is about: **giving thanks** for what is good, doing **penance**, that is, thinking about one's own mistakes, and **praying**. The day is a **state holiday**, not a purely church one. It is meant to unite people of different denominations. Since the **Second Vatican Council** (1962 to 1965), Catholic and Reformed congregations in many places celebrate **ecumenically** together.

A **Bettag proclamation** (Bettagsmandat) is a public appeal by the authorities for the Bettag. In it the authorities ordered the day and explained its meaning for the time in question. The writer **Gottfried Keller** was First State Secretary of the canton of **Zurich** from 1861 to 1876. His duties also included the Bettag proclamations. From the late 19th century, church texts increasingly took their place.

The canton of **Geneva** has its own tradition, the **Jeûne genevois**. It falls on the Thursday after the first Sunday in September. In **Vaud**, the Monday after the Bettag, the **Lundi du Jeûne**, is a public holiday. In Neuchâtel and in parts of the Bernese Jura this Monday is also a day off.

A well-known custom is the **plum tart** on the Bettag. It comes from the time when people were simply to eat and not cook for long on the Bettag. That way they had more time for the service. In September the **plums** are ripe, so this tart suited the day well. Many families still bake it on this Sunday today.

gewusst: The common Bettag is older than the Swiss federal state, which was only founded in 1848.
The Jeûne genevois recalls the news of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572 in France.

teile.einleitung: The Jesuit Article was a ban on the Jesuit order in the Swiss Federal Constitution. It applied from 1848 to 1973 and was one of the so-called confessional exception articles.
wichtigste: The ban on Jesuits first appeared in the Federal Constitution of 1848.
The Federal Constitution of 1874 tightened it in Article 51.
The Jesuits were forbidden any activity in church and school.
In 1973 the people and the cantons lifted the ban with about 54.9 per cent Yes.
In the same vote the ban on new monasteries also fell.
By today's view, the ban violated freedom of religion.

abschnitte.text: In the 1840s Switzerland was deeply divided between liberal and Catholic-conservative cantons. In 1844 the canton of **Lucerne** called the Jesuits to its higher school. Many liberals saw this as a threat. The dispute contributed to the **Sonderbund War** of 1847. After the victory of the liberals the federal state arose in 1848, and the **Federal Constitution of 1848** banned the Jesuit order.

In the 1870s there was a **Kulturkampf** in Switzerland, a dispute between the state and the Catholic Church. The new **Federal Constitution of 1874** tightened the ban. In **Article 51** any member of the order was forbidden any **activity in church and school**. In addition, Article 52 forbade the founding of new monasteries. Such rules are called **confessional exception articles**, because they concerned only one religious group.

In the 20th century criticism of these articles grew. They contradicted **freedom of religion**, that is, the right to live one's faith freely. In the 1960s Switzerland planned to join the **European Convention on Human Rights**. With the ban on Jesuits it would have had to enter reservations for this. That made the ban seem all the more problematic.

On 20 May 1973 the **people and the cantons** voted on the repeal. About **54.9 per cent** of those voting said Yes. In the same vote the **ban on new monasteries** was also lifted. A year later Switzerland joined the European Convention on Human Rights. The vote shows how the relationship between the denominations in Switzerland had eased.

gewusst: Even after 1848, individual Swiss Jesuits lived abroad and worked there as teachers or researchers.
The repeal was a constitutional amendment, so it needed the majority of the people and of the cantons.

teile.einleitung: John Calvin was a Reformer from France who worked mainly in Geneva. His teaching shaped the Reformed churches in many countries, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: Calvin was born in France in 1509.
His most important work is the “Institutio Christianae Religionis”, first published in 1536.
In 1538 he was expelled from Geneva and went to Strasbourg.
In 1541 he returned to Geneva.
In 1559 he founded the Geneva Academy.
The doctrine of predestination is especially associated with him.

abschnitte.text: Calvin was born in 1509 in Noyon in **France**. He studied law and theology and turned to the Reformation. Because Protestants were being persecuted in France, he fled. In 1536 he published in Basel the **Institutes of the Christian Religion**, an introduction to the Christian faith. In the same year the Reformer Guillaume Farel persuaded him to stay in **Geneva**.

In Geneva, Calvin wanted to introduce strict rules for the life of believers. Not everyone liked this, and in **1538** he was **expelled** from the city. He went to **Strasbourg** and looked after a congregation of French refugees there. In **1541** the people of Geneva called him back. After that he shaped the church and life in Geneva until his death in 1564.

For Calvin the **Bible** was at the centre. He stressed that God is almighty and that human beings are saved by God's grace alone. Especially well known is his teaching of **predestination**. It says that God has determined from the beginning who will be saved. Calvin also placed great value on a disciplined, hardworking life. In 1549 he agreed with Heinrich Bullinger of Zurich on a common teaching about the Lord's Supper.

In **1559** Calvin founded the **Geneva Academy**, from which the University of Geneva later arose. Pastors from many countries were trained there. They carried his teaching to France, the Netherlands, Scotland and beyond. That is why Geneva was often called the **Protestant Rome**. In Geneva today the great Reformation Wall in the Parc des Bastions recalls Calvin and other Reformers.

Calvin's Geneva was very strict. Whoever broke the rules was punished. Best known is the case of **Michael Servetus**, a Spanish doctor and theologian. He rejected the Trinity and was burned as a heretic in Geneva in **1553**. Calvin had supported the accusation. This case is still discussed critically today.

gewusst: Calvin's French name is Jean Cauvin.
In Geneva since 1903 there has been an expiatory monument to Michael Servetus, which followers of Calvin had erected.

teile.einleitung: The historical-critical method is a scholarly way of reading the Bible. It asks how the texts came about, who wrote them and what they meant in their own time.
wichtigste: The method arose above all since the Enlightenment in the 18th and 19th centuries.
It consists of several steps such as textual criticism, literary criticism, form criticism and redaction criticism.
Textual criticism looks for the oldest attainable wording of a text.
Julius Wellhausen shaped the documentary hypothesis on the five books of Moses.
Hermann Gunkel asked about the “setting in life” of a text.
Rudolf Bultmann shaped the form criticism of the New Testament and demythologisation.

abschnitte.text: There are no original manuscripts of the Bible, only many copies that differ in small details. **Textual criticism** compares these manuscripts and tries to restore the oldest attainable wording. In doing so, rules apply such as “lectio difficilior potior”: the **more difficult reading** is to be preferred. Copyists were more likely to smooth over difficult passages than to create new difficulties. An important step was the printed Greek edition of the New Testament by Erasmus of Rotterdam in 1516, which appeared in Basel.

**Literary criticism** asks whether a text is put together from older sources. For the five books of Moses, the **Pentateuch**, the **documentary hypothesis** developed in this way. Julius Wellhausen decisively shaped it in the 19th century. He distinguished four source documents with the abbreviations J, E, D and P and dated the Priestly source late. His view was authoritative for a long time, but is now often developed further.

**Form criticism** studies small units of text and their typical forms, for example Psalms, legends, parables or miracle stories. Hermann Gunkel founded this work on the Old Testament around 1900. He coined the term **setting in life**: the typical situation in which a form of text was used, such as a service or a festival. Rudolf Bultmann applied the approach to the Gospels. His work “The History of the Synoptic Tradition” appeared in 1921.

**Redaction criticism** sees the evangelists as independent authors. It asks how they selected, arranged and altered their sources in order to make their own theological statements. A classic is “The Theology of St Luke” by Hans Conzelmann from 1954, in German “Die Mitte der Zeit”, “The Middle of Time”. In it he shows that Luke divides history into epochs and presents the time of Jesus as the middle.

Rudolf Bultmann developed the programme of **demythologisation**. He did not want simply to throw away the mythical worldview of the New Testament, but to interpret it for people today. The historical-critical method is widespread at universities, including at the theological faculties in Switzerland. Some believers regard it critically, because it examines the Bible like other ancient books. Others find that it helps to understand the texts better.

gewusst: The word “critical” here does not mean “rejecting” but “examining closely”.
For some passages of the New Testament there are several thousand manuscripts that can be compared.

teile.einleitung: The Isenheim Altarpiece is one of the most famous works of art at the transition from the Middle Ages to the modern era. It was made for a monastery in Alsace and today stands in a museum in Colmar.
wichtigste: Matthias Grünewald painted the panels between about 1512 and 1516.
The altarpiece was made for the Antonites in Isenheim.
The Antonites cared for the sick with St Anthony's fire, which was caused by ergot.
It is a polyptych whose wings can be opened and closed.
John the Baptist points with a long index finger at the crucified Christ.
Today the altarpiece is on display in the Unterlinden Museum in Colmar.

abschnitte.text: The pictures of the altarpiece were painted by **Matthias Grünewald** between about 1512 and 1516. The carved figures inside come from the sculptor Niklaus of Haguenau. The altarpiece was commissioned by the monastery of the **Antonites** in **Isenheim** in Alsace. Today it stands in the **Unterlinden** Museum in **Colmar**, not far from Basel. Many visitors from Switzerland travel there to see it.

The Antonites were an order that looked after the sick. Many suffered from **St Anthony's fire**. This illness was caused by **ergot**, a poisonous fungus in grain, and caused burning pains. The sick were brought before the altarpiece. In the suffering Christ they were meant to see that God knows their pain and suffers with them.

The Isenheim Altarpiece is a **polyptych** with movable wings. Depending on the time in the church year, the wings were opened in different ways. So there are three different views, which are called **openings**. On ordinary days the first view, with the Crucifixion, was to be seen. On feast days the wings were opened and showed more cheerful pictures.

The Crucifixion is painted in a very striking way: Christ hangs heavily on the cross, his body marked with wounds. On the right stands **John the Baptist** and points at him with an **overlong index finger**. At his feet stands a **lamb with a cross**, a sign for Christ. John was in fact already dead at the time of the Crucifixion. The painter shows him all the same, because he points to Jesus.

On the second view the **Resurrection** is especially famous. Christ rises from the tomb in a shining light. Around him gleams a large coloured circle of light. The guards at the tomb fall to the ground, dazzled. This picture forms a strong contrast to the dark suffering of the Crucifixion.

gewusst: Little is known about the life of Matthias Grünewald, and his real name was probably Mathis Gothart Nithart.
Ergot was later also used for medicines, in small amounts and precisely dosed.

teile.einleitung: Confirmation (Firmung) is a sacrament of the Catholic Church. In it the faith that a person received in baptism is strengthened. Those being confirmed are meant to receive the power of the Holy Spirit.
wichtigste: “Firmung” comes from the Latin “confirmatio”, which means strengthening.
As a rule the bishop or his representative administers confirmation.
The forehead is anointed with the oil chrism.
Confirmation links especially to Pentecost.
Traditionally seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are named.
In Protestant churches there is Konfirmation.

abschnitte.text: The word **Firmung** comes from the Latin **“confirmatio”**. This means **strengthening** or reinforcement. The young person reaffirms their faith, and the Church believes that God strengthens them in doing so. Together with baptism and the Eucharist, confirmation is one of the three sacraments by which a person is fully received into the Church.

Confirmation links especially to **Pentecost**. According to the Bible, the **Holy Spirit** came down on the disciples of Jesus at Pentecost. After that they had the courage to tell people about their faith. Traditionally **seven gifts** of the Holy Spirit are named: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord.

As a rule the **bishop** or someone appointed by him administers confirmation. He lays his hand on the candidate and anoints their forehead with **chrism**. This is a consecrated oil with balsam that smells pleasant. In doing so he says: “Be sealed with the gift of God, the Holy Spirit.” The candidate answers “Amen”.

Each candidate has a special companion, the **confirmation sponsor**. This person lays a hand on the candidate's shoulder during the celebration. In Switzerland many young people are not confirmed until their teens. Before that they prepare in groups, for example with discussions and community service.

In **Protestant churches** there is a similar celebration too: **Konfirmation**. In it, young people confirm their baptism, which was usually in childhood. For the Protestant churches, however, Konfirmation is not a sacrament.

gewusst: Chrism is consecrated by the bishop every year in Holy Week.
Firmung and Konfirmation both come from the same Latin word.

teile.einleitung: The doctrine of grace is a part of Christian theology. It asks how a person finds their way to God and is saved: by their own strength or through God's **grace**, that is, an undeserved gift. In the history of the Church there has been a great deal of argument about this question.
wichtigste: In theology, grace means an undeserved gift from God.
The Synod of Orange taught in 529 that even the beginning of faith is a work of grace.
The Reformation stressed “sola gratia”, by grace alone.
John Calvin taught double predestination in Geneva.
The Synod of Dort confirmed Calvinist teaching in 1618/19.
In Jansenism and in the dispute over grace there were also fierce debates among Catholics.

abschnitte.text: As early as the 5th century, the Church Father **Augustine** argued with the monk Pelagius. Pelagius thought that people could live well by their own strength. Augustine, by contrast, stressed that people depend entirely on God's grace. The **Synod of Orange** taught in the year 529 that even the beginning of faith is a work of grace. In this way it confirmed the main outlines of Augustine's teaching.

The Reformers stressed the principle of **sola gratia**, which means “by grace alone”. Salvation is a gift of God that cannot be earned. The Reformer **John Calvin** taught **double predestination** in Geneva. According to this, God has predestined some to salvation and others to rejection. Calvin's teaching shaped the Reformed churches worldwide.

In the Netherlands, the **Remonstrants** followed the theologian Jacobus Arminius. They rejected unconditional election and stressed human freedom. The **Synod of Dort** in 1618/19 condemned their teaching. It confirmed the Calvinist doctrine of grace. Delegates from Switzerland also took part in the synod.

In the Catholic Church people speak of **sanctifying grace**, a lasting state of the soul. The Spanish Jesuit **Luis de Molina** developed the teaching of God's “middle knowledge” in order to reconcile God's foreknowledge with human freedom. **Jansenism**, centred on the convent of **Port-Royal**, by contrast held a strict Augustinian teaching. In 1653 Pope Innocent X condemned five propositions attributed to the Jansenists in the bull **Cum occasione**.

gewusst: The famous mathematician Blaise Pascal was close to the Jansenism of Port-Royal.
Jansenism goes back to the book “Augustinus” by Cornelius Jansen from the year 1640.

teile.einleitung: The Damascus experience is a story from the Bible. A man called Saul persecuted the Christians until he met Jesus on the road to Damascus. After that he became a Christian himself and was known as the apostle Paul.
wichtigste: Paul was also called Saul, which is what he is called at the start of the story.
At first Saul persecuted the followers of Jesus.
On the road to Damascus a bright light shone around him and he fell to the ground.
A voice said: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”
Saul was blind for three days and ate and drank nothing.
Ananias laid his hands on him, and then he could see again.
Later Paul escaped over the city wall of Damascus in a basket.

abschnitte.text: The story is found in the **Acts of the Apostles** in the New Testament. **Saul** came from the city of Tarsus and was a strictly religious Jew. He was against the followers of Jesus and wanted to take them prisoner. So he set out for **Damascus**, a large city in what is now Syria. There he wanted to track down Christians.

Shortly before Damascus, a **bright light** from heaven suddenly shone around him. Saul fell to the ground. Then he heard a voice: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” When he asked who was speaking, the voice answered: “I am **Jesus**, whom you are persecuting.” His companions heard the voice but saw no one.

When Saul got up, he could not see anything. His companions led him to Damascus. For **three days** he was blind and ate and drank nothing. Then God sent a disciple called **Ananias** to him. Ananias laid his hands on him, and it was as though **scales fell from Saul's eyes**. He could see again and was baptised.

Now Saul himself told people in Damascus about Jesus. This made some people angry, and they wanted to kill him. They guarded the **city gates** so that he could not escape. But his friends let him down over the city wall at night in a **basket**. In this way he was able to flee.

abschnitte.titel: Sayings that are still used today
abschnitte.text: Well-known **sayings** come from this story. In German, people say “It fell like scales from my eyes” when they suddenly understand something. “To go from Saul to Paul” means that someone completely changes their mind. And a **Damascus experience** is an event that fundamentally changes a person's life.

gewusst: Paul became one of the most important apostles and travelled widely around the Mediterranean region.
Many letters in the New Testament are attributed to Paul.

teile.einleitung: The story of David and Goliath is found in the Old Testament. The young shepherd David defeats the giant warrior Goliath with a sling. To this day the story stands for the victory of a small person over an apparently overwhelming opponent.
wichtigste: Goliath was a giant warrior of the Philistines.
David was a young shepherd who looked after his father's sheep.
He played the harp for King Saul.
Goliath wore a bronze helmet and heavy armour.
David took off Saul's armour because he could not walk well in it.
He chose five smooth stones from the brook and defeated Goliath with the sling.
Later David became king of Israel.

abschnitte.text: At that time the people of Israel were fighting the **Philistines**. The two armies faced each other in a valley. Among the Philistines there was a giant warrior called **Goliath**. He wore a **bronze helmet** and heavy armour. He challenged the Israelites to send one man to fight him. But everyone was afraid.

**David** was still young and looked after his father's **sheep**. In doing so he had learned to drive off wild animals. He could also play beautifully on the **harp**. When King **Saul** was sad, David played for him. When David heard about Goliath, he said that he wanted to fight him.

Saul wanted to give David his own **armour** and helmet. David put them on, but he was not used to them and could hardly walk in them. So he took them off again. He took only his shepherd's staff and his **sling**. At the brook he chose **five smooth stones** and put them in his shepherd's bag.

Goliath laughed at the young David. But David said that he came in the name of God. He put a stone in the sling and hit Goliath on the **forehead**. The giant fell to the ground. Without a sword and without armour, David had won. The Philistines fled.

After many years David became **king of Israel**. He made **Jerusalem** his capital. In the Bible many **psalms**, that is, prayers and songs, are attributed to him. The expression “David against Goliath” is used today when a small side takes on a big one, for example a small football club against a famous one.

gewusst: The artist Michelangelo created a marble statue of David more than four metres tall in Florence.
In the Bible Goliath's height is given as six cubits and a span, which would be almost three metres.

teile.einleitung: All Souls' Day is a Catholic day of remembrance on 2 November. On this day people remember all the people who have died and pray for them. The day follows directly after All Saints' Day.
wichtigste: All Souls' Day is on 2 November.
The day is devoted to remembering all the dead.
Abbot Odilo of Cluny introduced it in his monasteries around the year 998.
Many people put grave lights on the graves.
The liturgical colour is violet or black.
Since 1915 a priest may celebrate three Masses on All Souls' Day.

abschnitte.titel: A day for all the dead
abschnitte.text: **All Souls' Day** follows directly after All Saints' Day, on **2 November**. On All Saints' Day the Church honours the saints. On All Souls' Day, by contrast, people remember **all the people who have died**. Many think of grandparents, parents or friends who have died. People visit their graves and remember them.

The day of remembrance was introduced by **Abbot Odilo of Cluny** around the year **998**. Cluny was a very important monastery in France with many daughter houses. Odilo ordered the day of remembrance for the monasteries of his union. Later the whole **Western Church** adopted it. In this way All Souls' Day came to be celebrated in many countries of Europe.

According to **Catholic teaching**, the living can help the dead. Through **prayer** and **Masses** they are meant to support them on their way to God. In the service the priest wears **violet** or **black** vestments. These colours stand for mourning and penance. In 1915, during the First World War, Pope **Benedict XV** allowed all priests to celebrate **three Masses** on All Souls' Day.

On All Souls' Day many people put **grave lights** on the graves. The little lights often burn all night. They are a sign of **hope** for eternal light for the dead. In the evening many cemeteries therefore glow with a warm light. The graves have usually already been decorated with flowers for All Saints' Day.

In **Mexico**, around All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day, people celebrate the **Día de los Muertos**, the “Day of the Dead”. The festival is colourful and cheerful. Families decorate **altars** with marigolds, photos and food for their dead. Painted skulls made of sugar are also typical. Since 2008 the festival has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.

gewusst: The marigolds at the Mexican festival of the dead are said to show the way with their colour and scent.
Reformed churches do not have All Souls' Day. They often remember the dead on Eternity Sunday in November.

teile.einleitung: The Investiture Controversy was a great struggle for power in the Middle Ages between Pope and king. It was about the question of who may appoint bishops and abbots to their office.
wichtigste: Investiture means installation in an office.
At its core it was about the appointment of bishops and abbots by laymen, that is, by kings and princes.
In 1075 Pope Gregory VII set down the privileges of the Pope in the Dictatus Papae.
In 1076 he excommunicated King Henry IV.
In 1122 the Concordat of Worms ended the dispute.
After that the king conferred the secular rights with the sceptre.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages bishops and abbots were not only spiritual leaders. They often owned large estates and also had secular power. That is why kings liked to appoint them themselves, so that loyal people held these offices. This appointment is called **investiture**. Reformers in the Church thought that **laymen**, that is, non-clergy such as kings, should not give out Church offices.

In **1075**, in the **Dictatus Papae**, Pope **Gregory VII** set down in 27 principles what privileges the Pope has. It said, for example, that he could even depose emperors. King **Henry IV** would not stand for this and demanded the Pope's resignation. In response Gregory VII **excommunicated** him in **1076**. With this the king was shut out of the Church, and his subjects no longer felt bound to him.

Many princes now turned against Henry IV. To save his power, in the winter of 1077 he crossed the Alps to **Canossa** in Italy, where the Pope was staying. He appeared as a penitent in front of the castle and asked for forgiveness. The Pope lifted the ban. To this day people say “to **go to Canossa**” when someone has to humble themselves and ask for forgiveness.

The dispute went on even after Canossa. Only in **1122** did Emperor Henry V and Pope Callixtus II agree in the **Concordat of Worms**. The Church now elected the bishops and gave them **ring and staff** as a sign of spiritual office. The king conferred the secular rights and property with the **sceptre**. In this way spiritual and secular power were separated more clearly.

gewusst: A concordat is a treaty between the Pope and a state, and such treaties still exist today.
Henry IV is said to have waited three days in a penitent's robe in front of the castle at Canossa.

teile.einleitung: Heinrich Bullinger was an important Swiss Reformer. After the death of Huldrych Zwingli he led the **Reformed church in Zurich** for over 40 years. With his writings and letters he shaped the Reformation across Europe.
wichtigste: Bullinger was born in Bremgarten in 1504.
From 1523 he taught at the monastery school of Kappel am Albis.
In 1531 he succeeded Zwingli at the Grossmünster in Zurich.
As head of the Zurich church he bore the title Antistes.
His “Decades” are 50 Latin teaching sermons.
He died in Zurich in 1575 and left over 12,000 letters.

abschnitte.text: Heinrich Bullinger was born on 18 July **1504** in **Bremgarten** in what is now the canton of Aargau. He studied in Cologne and got to know the writings of the Reformers there. From **1523** he taught at the monastery school of **Kappel am Albis**. Abbot Wolfgang Joner had brought him there when he was only 19. In Kappel, Bullinger introduced a Reformation interpretation of the Bible.

In October 1531, **Zwingli** fell in the Battle of Kappel in the war against the Catholic cantons. In December **1531**, Zurich elected Bullinger, only 27 years old, as pastor of the **Grossmünster**. As head of the Zurich church he bore the title **Antistes**, which is Latin and means “head”. He led the Zurich church calmly and wisely through a difficult time. Bullinger remained in office until his death.

Bullinger wrote a great many books. His main work is the **Decades**, a collection of 50 Latin teaching sermons in five parts of ten each. They were also widely read in **England**. Bullinger wrote the **Second Helvetic Confession**, which is still important for many Reformed churches today. With John Calvin of Geneva he reached agreement in 1549 on the Lord's Supper in the Consensus Tigurinus.

Bullinger was in contact with scholars, pastors and princes all over Europe. **Over 12,000 letters** from and to him survive. This is one of the largest correspondences of the 16th century. He also took in refugees from other countries in Zurich. Heinrich Bullinger died in Zurich on 17 September **1575**.

gewusst: Bullinger's correspondence is still being studied and published at the University of Zurich today.
Bullinger's Second Helvetic Confession was adopted by Reformed churches in many countries.

teile.einleitung: The Gutenberg Bible is the first great book printed in Europe with movable metal type. **Johannes Gutenberg** printed it around **1452 to 1454** in Mainz. Today it is among the most valuable books in the world.
wichtigste: The Gutenberg Bible was printed around 1452 to 1454.
It was printed in Mainz.
A column usually has 42 lines, which is why it is also called the B42.
Around 180 copies were printed.
Today 49 copies survive in whole or in part.
It was printed on paper and partly on parchment.

abschnitte.text: Before Gutenberg, books were mostly copied out by hand, which often took years. In **Mainz** Gutenberg invented a process using **movable type** made of metal. Each letter was a separate piece and could be used again and again. With a **printing press**, many identical pages could be produced. Mainz lies on the Rhine in what is now the federal state of Rhineland-Palatinate.

Each page of the Gutenberg Bible has **two columns** with usually **42 lines**. That is why it is also called the 42-line Bible, or **B42** for short. It has about **1280 pages** in all and is divided into two large volumes. The text is in **Latin**. The typeface looks like the handwriting of the time.

About **180 copies** were printed, which was a large print run for the time. Most were made on **paper**, a smaller number on expensive **parchment** made of animal skin. Red headings and coloured decorations were added later **by hand**. That is why every copy looks a little different. As early as 1455, a scholar reported in a letter on finished sheets.

Today **49 copies** survive in whole or in part. Many others were lost over the centuries. The surviving Bibles are kept in large libraries and museums all over the world. Printing changed Europe greatly: books became cheaper, and knowledge could spread faster. Later this also helped the **Reformation**.

gewusst: In the Gutenberg Museum in Mainz you can see real copies of the Gutenberg Bible.
For the parchment copies, the skins of a great many calves were needed.

teile.einleitung: Joseph and his brothers is one of the best-known stories of the Bible. It tells how Joseph is sold by his brothers, becomes a powerful man in Egypt and in the end forgives his family.
wichtigste: Joseph's father was called Jacob.
Joseph had eleven brothers, the youngest was called Benjamin.
His father gave him a coat of many colours.
The brothers threw Joseph into an empty well and sold him to traders.
In Egypt Joseph interpreted the Pharaoh's dreams.
The seven lean cows meant seven years of famine.

abschnitte.text: **Jacob** had twelve sons. So Joseph had **eleven brothers**. Jacob loved Joseph especially and gave him a **coat of many colours**. This made the brothers jealous. Then there were Joseph's dreams: in one dream all the brothers were binding sheaves in the field, and **the brothers' sheaves** bowed down to Joseph's sheaf. The brothers became even angrier because of this.

One day the brothers were tending the flocks far away from home. When Joseph came to them, they stripped him of his coat and threw him into an **empty well**. Then **traders** passed by on their way to Egypt. The brothers **sold** Joseph to them. To their father they showed the coat, which they had smeared with animal blood. Jacob believed that a wild animal had killed Joseph.

In **Egypt** Joseph was sold as a servant. Later he was wrongly accused and ended up in prison. There he interpreted the dreams of two fellow prisoners, and his interpretations came true. When the **Pharaoh** had strange dreams, Joseph was sent for. The Pharaoh had seen seven fat and seven **lean cows**. Joseph explained: seven years of rich harvest are coming, and after them **seven years of famine**.

The Pharaoh was impressed and made Joseph his chief administrator. In the good years Joseph had a great deal of grain gathered in storehouses. When the famine came, Egypt had enough to eat. In other countries too people went hungry. So one day Joseph's brothers also came to Egypt to buy grain. They did not recognise Joseph.

Joseph tested his brothers. He wanted to see whether they had changed. He demanded that they bring their youngest brother **Benjamin**, and had a silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. When the brothers were ready to stand up for Benjamin, Joseph made himself known. He forgave them. The whole family moved to Egypt with Jacob.

gewusst: The story of Joseph was turned into a well-known musical by Andrew Lloyd Webber.
Thomas Mann wrote a great novel in four volumes about Joseph: “Joseph and His Brothers”.

teile.einleitung: Boniface was a monk from England who spread Christianity in present-day Germany in the 8th century. That is why he is called the “Apostle of the Germans”. He died in 754 in Frisia.
wichtigste: Boniface came from England and was originally called Winfrith.
He bears the epithet “Apostle of the Germans”.
Near Geismar he had an oak dedicated to the god Thor felled.
From 746 he was bishop in Mainz.
He was killed in 754 in Frisia.
His tomb is in Fulda, and his feast day is 5 June.

abschnitte.text: Boniface was born around 673 in **England**. His original name was **Winfrith**. Already as a child he came to a monastery and became a monk. He wanted to bring Christianity to the peoples on the continent. The pope gave him the name **Boniface**, which means roughly “the benefactor”.

At that time many people in Germania still venerated the old gods. Near **Geismar** in present-day Hesse stood a mighty **oak** dedicated to the god **Thor**. Boniface had it felled. Because the god did not punish him, according to tradition many people had themselves baptised. He is said to have built a chapel from the wood.

Boniface founded monasteries and set up dioceses. He put the Church in the Frankish kingdom in order and worked closely with the pope. From **746** he was bishop in **Mainz**. His pupil founded the monastery of **Fulda** on his behalf. Because of his great achievements Boniface bears the epithet **“Apostle of the Germans”**.

In old age Boniface travelled once more on a mission to **Frisia**, on the coast of the present-day Netherlands. There in **754** he was killed with his companions by opponents. His body was brought to **Fulda**. There his **tomb** lies in the cathedral. His feast day is **5 June**.

gewusst: The Catholic bishops of Germany meet every autumn in Fulda, at the tomb of Boniface.
Boniface left behind many letters, which have survived to this day.

teile.einleitung: Maundy Thursday (Gründonnerstag) is the Thursday before Easter. On this day Christians remember the **Last Supper**, which Jesus celebrated with his twelve disciples. After that he prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane and was arrested.
wichtigste: On Maundy Thursday Jesus celebrated the Last Supper.
His twelve disciples sat at the table with him.
After that Jesus prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane.
The disciples fell asleep there.
Judas betrayed Jesus with a kiss.
From Maundy Thursday the bells in Catholic churches are silent until the Easter Vigil.

abschnitte.text: On the evening before his death, Jesus ate one last time with his **twelve disciples**. He took bread and wine and said they should do this in his memory. Christians still remember this today in the **Lord's Supper** or the **Eucharist**. According to the Gospel of John, Jesus also washed his disciples' feet that evening. In this way he showed that people should serve one another.

After the meal Jesus went with the disciples to the Garden of **Gethsemane** outside Jerusalem. There he prayed, full of fear. He asked the disciples to stay awake with him, but they were tired and **fell asleep**. Then **Judas** came with soldiers. He greeted Jesus with a **kiss**, so the soldiers knew whom to arrest.

From Maundy Thursday the **bells** in Catholic churches are silent until the Easter Vigil. Children used to be told that the bells **fly to Rome**. In some places children go through the streets instead with **wooden rattles** or clappers. With the noise they call people to church. This custom also exists in some parts of Switzerland.

Where the name Gründonnerstag comes from is not quite certain. One explanation traces it back to the old word “greinen”, which means to weep. Because of the name, by old custom something **green** often goes on the table. **Spinach**, herb soup or green salad are popular. Maundy Thursday opens the three holy days before Easter.

gewusst: On Maundy Thursday the Pope traditionally washes the feet of twelve people.
Leonardo da Vinci's famous wall painting “The Last Supper” is in Milan.

teile.einleitung: Fyodor Dostoevsky was one of the most important writers of Russia. He lived from 1821 to 1881. His novels are often about guilt, suffering, faith and the question of God.
wichtigste: Dostoevsky was a Russian writer and a Russian Orthodox Christian.
In 1849 he went through a mock execution and was then exiled to Siberia.
In the prison camp the New Testament was his most important reading.
In “The Brothers Karamazov”, Ivan tells the story of the Grand Inquisitor.
Holbein's painting “The Body of the Dead Christ in the Tomb” in Basel shook him in 1867.
Prince Myshkin in “The Idiot” is conceived as a Christ figure.

abschnitte.text: As a young man, Dostoevsky belonged to a circle that discussed forbidden political ideas. In 1849 he was arrested and sentenced to death. Only at the last moment was it announced that the tsar had pardoned him. It was a **mock execution**. After that he had to spend several years in a prison camp in **Siberia**. There the **New Testament** was his most important reading.

Dostoevsky was a **Russian Orthodox** Christian. For him, Christ was the greatest model for people. But in his books he also asks difficult questions: why is there suffering if God is good? His characters doubt, argue and search for answers.

In the novel **“Crime and Punishment”** the student **Raskolnikov** commits a murder. After that his feelings of guilt torment him. The young woman **Sonya** reads him the Bible story of the **raising of Lazarus**. It is meant to show that a new life is possible even for him.

In 1867 Dostoevsky saw in the Kunstmuseum in **Basel** the painting **“The Body of the Dead Christ in the Tomb”** by **Hans Holbein**. It shows Jesus very realistically as a dead man. The picture shook him so much that it appears in the novel **“The Idiot”**. The main character of this novel, **Prince Myshkin**, is conceived as a “perfectly beautiful person” and a Christ figure.

His last great novel is **“The Brothers Karamazov”**. In it Ivan recites the tale of the **Grand Inquisitor**. Christ returns to **Seville** in it and is arrested. The youngest brother **Alyosha** has a wise teacher, the monk **Elder Zosima**. In the Orthodox Church an elder (starets) is an experienced spiritual guide.

gewusst: Dostoevsky had been given the New Testament in Siberia by the wives of exiled revolutionaries, and he kept it all his life.
His wife said that he climbed on a chair in the Basel museum to see the picture more closely.

teile.einleitung: Francis of Assisi was a saint from Italy. He lived around the year 1200 and gave up his wealth in order to live as poor as Jesus. He is especially known for his love of animals and of the whole of creation.
wichtigste: Francis of Assisi came from Italy.
He gave up his wealth in order to live as poor as Jesus.
According to one story, he preached to the birds.
The brothers who live after his example are called Franciscans.
In 1223 he set up a Christmas crib at Greccio.
He wrote the Canticle of the Sun.
His feast day, 4 October, is World Animal Day.

abschnitte.titel: From rich son to poor man
abschnitte.text: Francis was born around 1181 in **Assisi** in **Italy**. His father was a rich cloth merchant. As a young man Francis liked to party and dreamed of becoming a knight. After an illness and a time as a prisoner, his life changed. He gave up his **wealth** and wanted to live **as poor as Jesus**. He looked after the sick and the poor.

Soon other men joined him. They lived simply, preached and worked or begged for their food. From this the order of the **Franciscans** arose. His friend **Clare** founded an order for women. Francis died in 1226 and was canonised just two years later.

Francis saw brothers and sisters in all creatures. According to a famous story, he **preached to the birds**. In the town of **Gubbio** he is said to have tamed a **wolf** of which people were afraid. His feast day is **4 October**. This is also **World Animal Day**. In some churches animals are blessed on this day.

Francis wrote the **Canticle of the Sun**. In this song he praises God for **Brother Sun** and **Sister Moon**, for wind, water, fire and earth. It is one of the oldest poems in the Italian language. Today many people also read it as a call to protect nature.

In 1223 Francis set up a **Christmas crib** at **Greccio**, with a manger, an ox and a donkey. In this way he wanted to show how poor Jesus was when he was born. Since then cribs have been very popular at Christmas. In 2013 the new Pope chose his name after Francis of Assisi: **Pope Francis**.

gewusst: Francis was never a priest but remained a deacon all his life.
Francis of Assisi is one of the patron saints of Italy and of the environment.

teile.einleitung: “Paradise Lost” is a long poem by the English poet John Milton. It tells the biblical story of the Fall of Adam and Eve. The work is regarded as the most important epic poem in the English language.
wichtigste: John Milton published the epic in 1667.
At its centre is the Fall of Adam and Eve.
Milton had gone blind and dictated the verses to other people.
He wanted to “justify the ways of God to men”.
The word “pandemonium” goes back to Milton's name for the capital of Hell.
The work is written in unrhymed blank verse.
Johann Jakob Bodmer of Zurich translated it into German in 1732.

abschnitte.text: **John Milton** was an English poet and thinker. By about 1652 he had gone completely **blind**. Even so, he created his greatest work. He **dictated** the verses to helpers and family members, who wrote them down. “Paradise Lost” appeared in 1667. An **epic** is a very long narrative poem about great events.

Milton tells of **Satan's rebellion** against God and of the fall of the rebel angels into Hell. Then follows the story of **Adam and Eve** in the Garden of Eden. Satan tempts them to eat the forbidden fruit. In the end both must **leave Paradise**. With this, Milton wants to “justify the ways of God to men”.

In Hell the fallen angels build a capital. Milton called it **Pandaemonium**, formed from Greek words for “all demons”. From this name a word has come that we still know today: a **pandemonium** is a wild confusion full of noise and chaos. Satan himself is a very impressive figure in the epic.

Milton wrote his work in **blank verse**. This is a line with five stresses that does **not rhyme**. At that time it was usual for great poems to be rhymed. Milton deliberately defended giving up rhyme. He felt it let him tell his story more freely and more powerfully.

In 1671 a sequel appeared with the title **“Paradise Regained”**. In it Jesus resists the temptations of Satan in the wilderness. In Zurich, the scholar **Johann Jakob Bodmer** translated “Paradise Lost” into German in 1732. He defended Milton in a dispute with the Leipzig scholar Gottsched and so influenced German literature.

gewusst: The first edition of 1667 had ten books, the second of 1674 twelve.
A famous line of Satan's in the epic runs, roughly: “Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.”

teile.einleitung: The parable of the prodigal son is one of the best-known stories of Jesus. A young man squanders his inheritance and returns to his father poor. The father welcomes him with open arms, for God forgives gladly.
wichtigste: A father has two sons.
The younger one demands his inheritance and squanders it in a far country.
Poor and hungry, he has to look after pigs.
He decides to return to his father.
The father runs to meet him and holds a feast.
The older brother is furious about this.

abschnitte.text: A father has **two sons**. The younger one demands his **share of the inheritance**, even though his father is still alive. He goes to a far country. There he **squanders** all his money. When a famine comes, he has nothing left.

The son now has to **look after pigs** for a farmer. For Jews, pigs were regarded as unclean, so this was an especially humiliating job. He is so hungry that he would gladly eat the pigs' food. Then he thinks of his father. He decides to **return** and ask for forgiveness.

abschnitte.titel: The father runs to meet him
abschnitte.text: The father sees his son coming **from far away**. Full of compassion, he **runs to meet him** and embraces him. He has the best robe brought, puts a **ring** on his finger and gives him shoes. Then he has the **fattened calf** killed and holds a great feast. He says: my son was lost and is found.

The older son comes in from the field and hears the music. When he finds out why there is a celebration, he is **furious**. He has always worked faithfully and never been given a feast. His father explains to him that everything he has belongs to him, but that one must rejoice over the brother who has come home. With the parable Jesus shows: **God forgives gladly** and rejoices over everyone who turns back.

gewusst: The parable is found only in the Gospel of Luke, in chapter 15.
The painter Rembrandt showed the return of the prodigal son in a famous painting.

teile.einleitung: Confession is a sacrament in the Catholic Church. In it a person confesses his or her sins to a priest and receives forgiveness. Today it is also called the Sacrament of Reconciliation.
wichtigste: In the Catholic Church, confession is also called the Sacrament of Reconciliation.
Before confession, people think honestly about their own faults: the examination of conscience.
Confession involves contrition, admission, making amends and absolution.
The absolution is called absolution and only a priest may give it.
The seal of confession forbids the priest to repeat anything.
The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 prescribed at least one confession a year.

abschnitte.text: Before confession people take time to think honestly about their own behaviour. Where have I hurt others? Where have I acted wrongly? This thinking is called the **examination of conscience**. What matters here is **contrition**, that is, honest regret. Whoever regrets wants to do better in future.

In confession you **confess** your sins to the **priest**. The priest talks with the person and often gives advice. He also names a penance, for example a prayer or a good deed as **amends**. At the end he speaks the **absolution**, the release from sins. According to Catholic teaching, only a priest may give absolution.

What is said in confession stays secret. The **seal of confession** strictly forbids the priest to **repeat** anything he has heard. This applies without exception and for life. In this way people can speak openly. A priest who breaks the secret is severely punished by the Church.

In the past people usually confessed in the **confessional**, a small booth with a grille between priest and penitent. Today there are often confession conversations in a room as well. The **Fourth Lateran Council** prescribed in **1215** that Catholics should confess at least once a year. In the Reformed churches confession is not a sacrament, but there are pastoral conversations there too.

gewusst: The Orthodox churches also know confession as a sacrament.
In many large churches there are fixed times for confession, often in several languages.

teile.einleitung: The fish is one of the oldest signs of the Christians. In Greek the word for fish is “ichthys”, and in this word lies a short confession of faith.
wichtigste: “Ichthys” is the Greek word for fish.
The letters stand for the words “Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour”.
The first Christians were at times persecuted and used the fish as a sign of recognition.
You can draw the sign with two curved lines.
Today the fish is sometimes seen as a sticker on the back of cars.

abschnitte.text: The New Testament was written in **Greek**, and many early Christians spoke this language. The Greek word for fish is **ichthys** and consists of five letters. Each letter is the beginning of a word: Iesous, Christos, Theou, Hyios, Soter. Translated, that means: “**Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour**”. In this way a simple word became a short confession of faith.

abschnitte.titel: A sign for recognising one another
abschnitte.text: In the first centuries, Christians in the Roman Empire were at times **persecuted**. So it was helpful to have a sign that only those in the know understood. An old story tells that one Christian drew an arc **in the sand**. The other added the second arc, and so a fish appeared. Whether it was exactly like that is not known, but the sign is found already in early Christian burial places.

Fish appear often in the Gospels. Some of Jesus's disciples were **fishermen** on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus said to them that he would make them **fishers of men**. By this he meant that they should win other people for his message. Also well known is the story in which Jesus feeds many people with a few loaves and fishes.

Today the fish is no longer a secret sign. Many Christians wear it as a pendant or stick it **on the back of the car**. In this way they openly show that they believe in Jesus. Churches, schools and Christian groups also use it as a logo. The sign is simple, because you can draw it with just **two lines**.

gewusst: Ichthys is a kind of acrostic: the initial letters of several words make a new word.
The fish sign is older than the cross as a widespread Christian symbol.

teile.einleitung: Benedict of Nursia was a monk in Italy who lived from about 480 to 547. He founded the monastery of Monte Cassino and wrote a famous rule for monastic life. He is regarded as the father of Western monasticism.
wichtigste: Benedict came from Nursia in central Italy.
For some years he lived as a hermit in a cave near Subiaco.
He founded the monastery of Monte Cassino.
His twin sister was Scholastica.
Pope Gregory the Great wrote a biography of him.
Since 1964 Benedict has been patron saint of Europe, and his feast day is 11 July.
