abschnitte.text: Benedict was born around 480 in **Nursia**, present-day Norcia in Italy. He went to Rome to study, but he did not like life there. He withdrew and lived for some years as a **hermit** in a cave near **Subiaco**. Soon men came to him who wanted to live as he did. In this way the first small monasteries arose.

Around 529 Benedict founded the monastery of **Monte Cassino** on a mountain. For his monks he wrote a rule, the **Rule of Saint Benedict**. Benedict died there around 547. In the Second World War the monastery was **destroyed by bombs in 1944**, because there was heavy fighting in the area. Afterwards it was rebuilt on the old model.

Benedict's **twin sister Scholastica** also led a spiritual life as a nun. What we know about Benedict comes mainly from Pope **Gregory the Great**. A few decades after Benedict's death he wrote a biography. In it he also tells many miracle stories about him.

The monks who live by Benedict's rule are called **Benedictines**. After their name stands the abbreviation **OSB**, Latin **Ordo Sancti Benedicti**, Order of Saint Benedict. They are also called **“black monks”**, because of their black habit. The head of a monastery is called an **abbot**. With the promise of **stability** they bind themselves to their monastery for life.

Benedictine monasteries have strongly shaped Europe. Monks copied books, preserved knowledge, laid out gardens and taught. That is why Pope Paul VI named Benedict **patron saint of Europe** in **1964**. The Catholic Church celebrates his feast on **11 July**. In Switzerland, for example, Einsiedeln, Engelberg and Disentis are Benedictine monasteries.

gewusst: According to tradition, Benedict died standing in prayer, supported by his monks.
The Rule of Saint Benedict has been followed in monasteries all over the world for almost 1,500 years.

teile.einleitung: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the oldest Christian churches in the world. It arose in the 4th century in the kingdom of Aksum in present-day Ethiopia. It has its own ancient traditions, festivals and even books in its Bible.
wichtigste: Tewahedo means “oneness” in Ge'ez.
The first bishop of Aksum, in the 4th century, was Frumentius.
The liturgy is celebrated in the ancient language Ge'ez.
In Lalibela there are famous churches hewn out of the rock.
Since 1959 the Church has had a patriarch of its own.
The great festival of Timkat recalls the baptism of Jesus.

abschnitte.text: The word **Tewahedo** comes from the ancient language **Ge'ez** and means **oneness**. It describes the oneness of the divine and human natures in Christ. This teaching is called **miaphysite**. The Church thus belongs to the Oriental Orthodox churches, like the Coptic Church in Egypt, for example.

In the 4th century the Syrian Christian **Frumentius** came to the court of **Aksum** as a shipwrecked man. He converted King **Ezana** to Christianity. **Athanasius** of Alexandria ordained him as the first bishop of the kingdom. For centuries afterwards the Coptic Church supplied the bishop of Ethiopia. Only in **1959** was the first Ethiopian **patriarch**, Abuna Basilios, installed.

**Ge'ez** was the language of the kingdom of Aksum. Today it is only a **church language** and is used in the liturgy. The present-day languages **Amharic** and **Tigrinya** are related to it. The Church's Bible also includes the **Book of Enoch**. It survives in full only in Ge'ez.

abschnitte.titel: Rock churches and the Ark of the Covenant
abschnitte.text: In the 12th and 13th centuries famous churches were hewn out of the rock in **Lalibela**. They are named after King Lalibela and were meant to represent a “new Jerusalem”. Since 1978 they have been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. According to Ethiopian tradition, the church of Mary in **Aksum** keeps the **Ark of the Covenant**. Only a single monk may see it.

In January the Church celebrates the great festival of **Timkat**. It recalls the **baptism of Jesus**. In it, the **tabots**, replicas of the tablets of the law, are carried to the water in solemn processions. Thousands of people in white robes join in the celebration. The festival is part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.

gewusst: According to the national epic Kebra Nagast, Menelik, son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, brought the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia.
Every Ethiopian Orthodox church owns a tabot. Only it makes the building a church.

teile.einleitung: Cain and Abel are two brothers from the first book of the Bible, Genesis. Their story tells of envy and anger between siblings. It is among the best-known stories of the Old Testament.
wichtigste: Cain and Abel were sons of Adam and Eve.
Abel was a shepherd, Cain was a farmer.
Both brought God an offering.
God looked favourably on Abel's gift, and Cain became angry about it.
Cain killed his brother Abel.
God asked: “Where is your brother Abel?”
God gave Cain a mark so that no one would kill him.

abschnitte.text: According to the Bible, **Adam and Eve** were the first people. Their sons were called **Cain** and **Abel**. Abel became a **shepherd**, so he tended animals. Cain became a **farmer** and worked the fields. The two occupations stand for two ancient ways of life of human beings.

Both brothers brought God an **offering**. Cain brought fruits from the field, Abel the best animals from his flock. God **looked favourably on Abel's gift**, but not on Cain's. The Bible does not say exactly why. Cain became **angry** and envious about this, and God warned him to master his anger.

Cain did not heed the warning. In the field he attacked his brother and **killed Abel**. After that God asked: **“Where is your brother Abel?”** Cain answered: **“Am I my brother's keeper?”** With this answer he wanted to talk his way out. It became a well-known phrase for people who do not want to take responsibility.

As a punishment Cain had to leave his land and wander restlessly. Cain feared that someone would now kill him. So God gave him a **mark** that protected him. This mark is called the **mark of Cain**. The story shows that even someone who has done something terrible remains under God's protection.

gewusst: The phrase “mark of Cain” is today also used for a visible sign of guilt.
According to the Bible, Adam and Eve later had another son named Seth.

teile.einleitung: The pulpit is a raised place in the church from which preaching is done. It often stands by a pillar or against a wall. From there the pastor speaks to the whole congregation.
wichtigste: Preaching is done from the pulpit.
The pulpit is raised so that everyone can hear and see well.
You climb up by a small staircase.
The roof above the pulpit is called a sounding board and directs the voice downwards.
In Reformed churches the pulpit is especially important.
The Bible often lies on the pulpit.

abschnitte.text: From the **pulpit** the pastor gives the **sermon**. In the sermon a text from the **Bible** is explained and applied to life today. That is why a Bible often lies on the desk of the pulpit. The pulpit stands **raised** so that everyone can hear and see well. In the past there were no microphones yet, so this was very important.

You get up to the pulpit by a **small staircase**. The part where the preacher stands often looks like a **basket** with a railing. In many churches the pulpit is attached to a **pillar** or to a **wall**. Many old pulpits are made of wood or stone and beautifully decorated. Some show pictures of saints or biblical scenes.

Above many pulpits hangs a small roof. It is called a **sounding board**. It **directs the voice downwards** to the listeners so that it is not lost in the high space of the church. In this way the sermon can be understood further back too. Sounding boards are often artistically designed, sometimes with a dove as a sign of the Holy Spirit.

In **Reformed churches** the pulpit is especially important. The Reformers such as Zwingli in Zurich put the **Word of God** and the sermon at the centre of the service. That is why the pulpit there often stands clearly visible at the front or in the middle. In Catholic churches, by contrast, the **altar** is the most important place. Today people often also preach from a simple lectern, the ambo.

gewusst: The German expression “jemanden abkanzeln” means to scold someone sharply, as was done in the past from the pulpit (Kanzel).
The German word Kanzel comes from the Latin “cancelli”, which means barriers or lattice.

teile.einleitung: The dove of peace is a white dove with an olive branch in its beak. It is a sign of peace all over the world. Its story begins in the Bible, with Noah and the ark.
wichtigste: After the Flood, Noah sent birds out from the ark.
First a raven flew out, then the dove.
The dove brought back an olive branch.
From this Noah realised that the water was going down.
The branches come from the olive tree.
Pablo Picasso drew a well-known dove of peace.

abschnitte.text: The Bible tells of a great **Flood**. Noah built an **ark**, a large ship. In it he saved his family and many animals. When the rain had stopped, Noah wanted to know whether the earth was dry again. First he let a **raven** fly out. After that he sent out a **dove**.

The first time, the dove found nowhere to settle and came back. The second time it brought a fresh **olive branch** in its beak. From this Noah realised that **the water was going down**. The third time the dove did not come back at all. That meant that it had found **dry land**. Soon everyone could leave the ark.

The branches that the dove of peace carries grow on the **olive tree**. Olive oil is pressed from its fruit. Olive trees grow all around the Mediterranean and can become very old. Even in ancient times the olive branch was a sign of peace.

Today a **white dove with an olive branch** is a sign of **peace**. The painter **Pablo Picasso** drew a famous dove. In 1949 it became the poster for a great peace congress in Paris. After that the dove became known all over the world. It is seen on posters, flags and stamps.

gewusst: Picasso named one of his daughters Paloma, which is the Spanish word for dove.
In Christianity the dove is also a sign of the Holy Spirit.

teile.einleitung: Icons are painted holy images, above all in the Orthodox churches. They show Jesus, Mary, saints or scenes from the Bible and are venerated in prayer.
wichtigste: The word comes from the Greek “eikon” and means image.
Icons are traditionally painted on wooden panels.
The paint is usually egg tempera, a paint made with egg yolk.
The golden background stands for heavenly light.
In the Byzantine Empire there was a long dispute over images.
Andrei Rublev painted the famous Trinity icon.

abschnitte.text: The word **icon** comes from the Greek **eikon** and simply means **image**. It refers to holy images, as they are especially important in the **Orthodox Church**, for example in Greece, Russia, Serbia or Romania. For believers an icon is more than a work of art. It is regarded as a kind of window onto the world of God. That is why people light candles in front of it and kiss it.

Icons are traditionally painted on **wooden panels**. The wood is first prepared with a white ground layer. Painting is done with **egg tempera**: coloured powder is mixed with egg yolk. Many icons have a **golden background**. It stands for **heavenly light** and shows that the saints are with God.

Icon painters keep to old models and strict rules. Faces, clothes and colours have fixed meanings. For example, Mary is often painted with a dark red mantle. The figures look flat and calm, because they are meant to show not the everyday world but the eternal. That is why people often say that an icon is not painted but **written**.

In the 8th and 9th centuries there was fierce argument in the **Byzantine Empire** over whether holy images may be venerated. This dispute is called **Iconoclasm**. The opponents of images feared that images might be worshipped like idols. Many icons were destroyed at that time. In 843 the veneration of images was finally permitted, and the Orthodox churches celebrate this to this day as the **Feast of Orthodoxy**.

One of the most famous icons is the **Trinity icon** by the Russian painter **Andrei Rublev** from the early 15th century. It shows three angels at a table, who are interpreted as an image of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Today it hangs in Moscow. In Orthodox churches many icons are placed on a large screen of images in front of the sanctuary, the **iconostasis**. In Switzerland too there are Orthodox congregations with such icons.

gewusst: Some icons are over 1,400 years old, for example in St Catherine's Monastery on the Sinai peninsula.
On many icons, people are identified by abbreviations of their names in Greek or Church Slavonic lettering.

teile.einleitung: Ash Wednesday is the start of Lent, the period before Easter. On this day priests mark many people's foreheads with a cross of ash. Shortly before it, the cheerful carnival ends in many places.
wichtigste: Ash Wednesday always falls 46 days before Easter Sunday.
It falls in February or March.
In church, many people receive a cross of ash on the forehead.
The ash often comes from burnt palm branches of the previous year.
The cross of ash is a sign of repentance and a new start.
On this day of fasting, Catholics eat no meat, but fish is allowed.
The Basel Carnival begins only on the Monday after Ash Wednesday.

abschnitte.text: Ash Wednesday depends on the **date of Easter**. It is always **46 days** before Easter Sunday. That is why it moves from year to year. It always falls in **February** or **March**. With Ash Wednesday **Lent** begins. It lasts 40 days if you do not count the Sundays.

In church the priest marks many people's foreheads with a little **cross of ash**. That is where the day gets its name. The ash often comes from the blessed **palm branches** of the previous year. They are burnt, and the ash is blessed. The cross of ash is a sign of **repentance** and a **new start**. It recalls that you can rethink your life.

For **Catholics**, Ash Wednesday is a **day of fasting**. People eat less and give up **meat**. **Fish** is allowed. That is why on this day there are fish dishes in many families and restaurants. In Lent too, many people give up something, for example sweets or their mobile phone.

Before the serious Ash Wednesday, many people celebrate cheerfully once more with masks and music. In many places the **carnival** ends shortly before Ash Wednesday, for example in **Lucerne**. An exception is the **Basel Carnival**. It begins only on the **Monday after Ash Wednesday**, at 4 in the morning with the **Morgestraich**. It is therefore later than most other carnivals.

gewusst: At the Morgestraich in Basel, all the street lamps in the city centre are put out at 4 in the morning.
Since 2017 the Basel Carnival has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.

teile.einleitung: Evangelicalism is a worldwide movement within Protestant Christianity. Evangelicals stress personal conversion, the Bible and passing on the faith. Important meetings of the movement have also taken place in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Evangelicals stress conversion, the Bible, the cross and activism.
In 1846 the Evangelical Alliance was founded in London.
In 1974 the International Congress on World Evangelization took place in Lausanne.
Billy Graham was largely responsible for inviting people to this congress.
John Stott led the drafting of the Lausanne Covenant.
In German-speaking Switzerland the Swiss Evangelical Alliance represents many evangelical churches and organisations.

abschnitte.text: The historian **David Bebbington** names four marks of evangelicalism. First, **conversion**: a person should consciously decide to believe in Jesus. Second, the **Bible** as the most important foundation. Third, the **cross**, that is, the death of Jesus as the centre of faith. Fourth, **activism**: Christians should actively live out their faith and pass it on.

The movement has its roots in the revival movements of the 18th and 19th centuries. From about 1816 the **Réveil** spread from Geneva through western Switzerland. In 1846 the **Evangelical Alliance** was founded in **London**. It was the first international union of Protestant Christians from different churches.

From 1910 to 1915 the series of booklets **“The Fundamentals”** appeared in the USA. A movement that was faithful to the Bible was named after it, **fundamentalism**. It stresses that the Bible is literally true. Many evangelicals later distanced themselves from this strict approach.

In 1974 the International Congress on World Evangelization took place in **Lausanne**. The American evangelist **Billy Graham** had largely been behind the invitation. Thousands of participants from many countries came. The Anglican theologian **John Stott** led the drafting of the **Lausanne Covenant**. It links proclaiming the faith with working for justice. In 1989 a second congress followed in **Manila**, which adopted a manifesto.

In German-speaking Switzerland the **Swiss Evangelical Alliance** represents numerous evangelical churches and organisations. These include many free churches, but also groups within the Reformed national churches. Evangelical Christians often shape their services with modern music. Some questions, such as how to interpret the Bible, are judged differently in public.

gewusst: The Lausanne Movement arose from the congress of 1974 and is still named after the city of Lausanne today.
In his life, Billy Graham spoke to many millions of people.

teile.einleitung: The Christ Catholic Church of Switzerland is a Catholic church of its own that is not under the Pope. It came into being after 1870, when Catholics rejected the new teaching of papal infallibility. It is the smallest of the three national churches of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Christ Catholics rejected papal infallibility, which the First Vatican Council proclaimed in 1870.
In 1871 opponents of this teaching met in Solothurn for the first Catholic congress.
In 1875 the Christ Catholic Church of Switzerland was organised.
The first bishop was Eduard Herzog, who was consecrated in 1876.
The bishop has his seat in Bern.
Outside Switzerland the sister churches are usually called Old Catholic.
Priests may marry, and women can also become priests.

abschnitte.titel: How the church came into being
abschnitte.text: In 1870 the **First Vatican Council** declared that the Pope is **infallible** in matters of faith. Some Catholics did not want to accept this teaching. In Switzerland they met in September 1871 in **Solothurn** for the first Swiss Catholic congress. From this a church of its own arose, which organised itself in 1875 as the **Christ Catholic Church of Switzerland**.

The first bishop was **Eduard Herzog**. He was consecrated in 1876 and led the church for almost 50 years. The bishop has his seat in **Bern**. Important decisions are made by the **National Synod**, where clergy and lay people discuss together. Christ Catholic theologians are trained at the University of Bern.

Similar churches also arose in other countries. In Germany, Austria and the Netherlands they are called **Old Catholic**. The name “Christ Catholic” is a Swiss speciality. In 1889 these churches joined together to form the **Union of Utrecht**, named after the Dutch city of Utrecht.

Christ Catholic priests do not have to live unmarried, as there is no **celibacy**. Since 1999, women in Switzerland can also be ordained as **priests**. The Christ Catholics were already celebrating services in the **national language** instead of Latin in the 19th century. The Roman Catholic Church only did this after the Second Vatican Council.

In several cantons the Christ Catholic Church is recognised as a **national church**, alongside the Roman Catholic and the Reformed churches. This means it has public-law recognition and can, for example, receive church taxes. But it is the smallest of the three national churches. There are congregations mainly in the cantons of Aargau, Solothurn, Bern and Basel.

gewusst: The Christ Catholics came into being at a time of great tension between the state and the Catholic Church, which is called the Kulturkampf.
In Bern, the Christ Catholic church of St Peter and Paul stands right next to the town hall.

teile.einleitung: On Ascension Day, Christians remember that Jesus returned to God in heaven after his resurrection. In Switzerland the holiday is usually called simply “Auffahrt”. It always falls on a Thursday.
wichtigste: Auffahrt commemorates the fact that Jesus was taken up into heaven.
The feast falls on the 40th day of the Easter season, counting Easter Sunday.
Auffahrt therefore always falls on a Thursday.
According to the Acts of the Apostles, a cloud took Jesus up before the eyes of the disciples.
According to the Bible, the place of the Ascension is the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem.
Auffahrt is a public holiday in all cantons of Switzerland.
In Beromünster LU, a large procession on horseback through the fields takes place on Ascension Day.

abschnitte.text: The **Acts of the Apostles** tells that after Easter Jesus showed himself to his disciples for 40 days. Then he was lifted up before their eyes, and a **cloud** took him up. This happened on the **Mount of Olives**, which lies right next to Jerusalem. After that the disciples returned to the city. The Gospel of Luke also tells of this briefly.

Auffahrt falls on the **40th day** of the Easter season, if you count Easter Sunday as the first day. That is exactly five weeks and four days after Easter. This is why the feast always falls on a **Thursday**. Because Easter is on a different date every year, Auffahrt also moves around the calendar. Ten days after Auffahrt comes Pentecost.

In Switzerland, Ascension Day is usually called **Auffahrt**. The day is a holiday in **all cantons**, just like Christmas. Many people also take the Friday after off and make a **bridge**. This makes a long weekend, which many people use for trips and holidays.

In **Beromünster** in the canton of Lucerne there is a very old custom, the **Auffahrtsumritt**. Riders, together with clergy, move in a long procession around the fields near the village. On the way there is praying and singing. People ask for protection and blessing for the **fields and the harvest**. Many spectators come every year to see the procession.

gewusst: In art, pictures of the Ascension often show only the feet of Jesus disappearing into a cloud.
Other places in the canton of Lucerne, such as Hitzkirch, also have an Auffahrt ride.

teile.einleitung: The “Institutio Christianae Religionis” is the main work of the Reformer John Calvin. The Latin title means roughly “Instruction in the Christian Religion”. The book became the most important foundation of Reformed teaching.
wichtigste: The first edition appeared in 1536 in Basel.
Calvin dedicated the work to King Francis I of France.
Calvin revised and expanded the book several times.
The final Latin version in four books appeared in 1559.
In 1541 Calvin himself translated the Institutes into French.

abschnitte.text: John Calvin fled from France as a young man, because Protestants were being persecuted there. In **Basel** he found refuge and published the first edition of the **Institutes** there in **1536**. He was then only about 26 years old. The first edition was still a fairly small book and explained the basics of the faith, such as the Ten Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer.

Calvin put a famous **preface addressed to King Francis I of France** at the front of the book. In it he defended the persecuted Protestants. He wanted to show that they were not rebels, but had a faith that rested on the Bible. The king, however, was not persuaded.

Calvin went on working on the Institutes all his life. With each edition it became larger. In **1541** he translated it himself into **French**, so that people without Latin could read it too. This translation is regarded as an important work of the French language. The Latin **final version of 1559** is divided into **four books**: on God the Creator, on Christ the Redeemer, on the work of the Holy Spirit and on the Church.

gewusst: The first edition had six chapters, the final version of 1559 has 80 chapters.

teile.einleitung: Athos is a mountain and a peninsula in the north of Greece. There lies an Orthodox monastic republic with 20 great monasteries. Monks have lived on Athos for over a thousand years, and women may not set foot on the peninsula.
wichtigste: The monastic republic of Athos consists of 20 great monasteries.
The ban on women is called the Avaton.
The seat of administration is the town of Karyes.
The oldest and highest-ranking monastery is Megisti Lavra, founded in 963.
Since 1988 Athos has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
In spiritual matters Athos is subject to the Ecumenical Patriarchate.
Pilgrims need a permit, the Diamonitirion.

abschnitte.text: **Athos** lies on a peninsula in the north of **Greece**. There **20 great monasteries** form the **monastic republic of Athos**. The monasteries have equal rights and share the whole peninsula. There are also numerous smaller monastic settlements and **hermitages** that belong to the monasteries. The monks live according to the rules of the **Orthodox** Church.

Athos is an **autonomous region** under Greek sovereignty. The seat of administration is **Karyes** in the middle of the peninsula. The representatives of the monasteries meet there, and the Greek **civil governor** also has his seat there. The port of Athos is called **Dafni**. In church matters, Athos is directly subject to the **Ecumenical Patriarchate** in Istanbul and not to the Greek national church.

The oldest and highest-ranking monastery is **Megisti Lavra**. It was founded in **963** by **Athanasius the Athonite**. Other monasteries are linked with particular peoples. **Hilandar** was founded in **1198** by **Sava** and his father **Stefan Nemanja** for Serbian monks. It is still a centre of Serbian culture today. **Zografou** has a Bulgarian character and **Panteleimon** a Russian one.

Women may not set foot on Athos. This ban is called the **Avaton**. It has applied for centuries and is anchored in Athos's **special status**. According to tradition it even concerns female domestic animals. Male pilgrims need a special permit, the **Diamonitirion**. It is issued only in limited numbers each day. Non-Orthodox visitors receive even fewer places than Orthodox pilgrims.

Since **1988** Athos has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. It was listed as a **mixed World Heritage Site**, that is, as cultural and natural heritage at once. What is honoured are the old **monastery buildings** with their art treasures and the unspoilt **landscape**. In the monasteries' libraries lie many thousands of ancient manuscripts.

gewusst: The mountain Athos at the southern tip of the peninsula is over 2,000 metres high.
In some Athos monasteries the clocks still follow the old Byzantine time, in which the day begins at sunset.

teile.einleitung: The Divine Comedy is a famous poem by the Italian poet **Dante Alighieri**. It describes an imaginary journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise. The work is regarded as one of the most important in world literature.
wichtigste: The Divine Comedy has three parts: Hell, Purgatory and Paradise.
It has 100 cantos in all.
The poet Virgil guides Dante through Hell and Purgatory.
Beatrice guides him through Paradise.
Dante wrote in tercets and in Italian instead of Latin.
All three parts end with the word “stelle”, stars.

abschnitte.text: Dante Alighieri lived in **Florence** and was also a politician there. In **1302** he was banished from his home city and never returned. In exile he wrote his great work. He simply called it “Commedia”, because it ends well. The word “divine” was only added later.

The journey begins in **Hell**, which is built like a huge funnel with nine circles. The deeper you go, the heavier the sins of the people there. Dante is guided by the Roman poet **Virgil**. At the lowest point **Lucifer**, the devil, is stuck, frozen in **ice**. Dante describes the punishments in detail, but as images of the consequences of sin.

After that Dante and Virgil climb **Mount Purgatory**. There, according to Catholic belief, souls are cleansed of their sins. In **Paradise** Dante is guided by **Beatrice**, a woman whom he greatly revered. Together they travel through the heavenly spheres up to God. All three parts end with the word **“stelle”**, which means stars.

The work has **100 cantos**: one introductory canto and three times 33 cantos. Dante used the **terza rima**, a stanza of three lines with the rhyme scheme aba bcb cdc. Around 1300, learned works were mostly written in **Latin**. Dante, by contrast, wrote in **Italian**, the language of ordinary people. That is why he is regarded as the father of the Italian language.

gewusst: The number three plays a big role in the Divine Comedy, as a sign of the Trinity.
Dante died in 1321 in Ravenna, where his tomb still stands today.

teile.einleitung: The Dominicans are a Catholic order that was founded in the 13th century. Their most important task is preaching, which is why they are also called the Order of Preachers. Many important scholars of the Middle Ages were Dominicans.
wichtigste: The order was founded by Dominic of Castile in Spain.
Pope Honorius III confirmed the order in the year 1216.
The abbreviation “OP” stands for Ordo Praedicatorum, the Order of Preachers.
The famous theologian Thomas Aquinas was a Dominican.
From the name came the play on words “Domini canes”, hounds of the Lord.

abschnitte.text: **Dominic**, in Spanish Domingo de Guzmán, came from Caleruega in **Castile**. He travelled to southern France and preached there. He wanted to win over people who had departed from the teaching of the Church through good sermons and a simple life. From this his community grew. Pope **Honorius III** confirmed the order in December **1216**.

The official name is **Ordo Praedicatorum**, that is, Order of Preachers. That is why Dominicans write **“OP”** after their names. The brothers were to be well educated so that they could preach convincingly. They belong to the **mendicant orders**: originally they owned hardly any property and lived on donations. They mostly built their monasteries in the **towns**, where many people lived.

The Dominicans placed great value on **education** and taught at the new universities. The best known is **Thomas Aquinas**. He joined the order against the wishes of his family. In his **“Summa Theologiae”** he combined the philosophy of Aristotle with Christian teaching. His teacher Albertus Magnus and the mystic Meister Eckhart were also Dominicans.

From the name came the Latin play on words **“Domini canes”**, hounds of the Lord. It portrays the brothers as **watchdogs** who protect the flock from false teaching. That is why their emblem often shows a dog with a **torch** in its mouth. In Switzerland, for example, the **Predigerkirchen** (Preachers' churches) in Zurich and Basel recall former Dominican monasteries.

gewusst: The Dominican dress is a white habit with a black cloak.
Dominic died in the year 1221 in Bologna, where he is buried to this day.

teile.einleitung: A creed sums up in a few sentences what Christians believe. After its Latin opening word it is also called the **Credo**, which means “I believe”. The best-known creeds are the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed.
wichtigste: The creed is named Credo after its first Latin word.
In it Christians profess faith in Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
The Roman governor Pontius Pilate is named in it.
The early Christians spoke a creed especially at baptism.
The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed was expanded in 381 and is accepted almost everywhere.
The Eastern and Western churches argued over the word Filioque.

abschnitte.text: The Latin word **Credo** means “I believe”. The creed begins with this word in Latin. Another technical term for it is **symbolum**, which means a sign of recognition. The early Christians spoke a creed especially at **baptism**. Whoever was baptised thereby said publicly what they believe.

The creed has three parts. It speaks of belief in God the **Father**, in Jesus Christ the **Son** and in the **Holy Spirit**. This teaching is called the Trinity. In the part about Jesus, **Pontius Pilate** is also named, the Roman governor under whom Jesus was crucified. In this way the faith is tied to a real point in history.

In the West the **Apostles' Creed** is very widespread. An old legend tells that each of the **twelve apostles** contributed one sentence to it. In reality it arose gradually from early baptismal creeds of the Church of Rome. It is often spoken together in Catholic and Reformed services.

In the year 325, bishops met in **Nicaea** for a council. Their creed was written in **Greek**, the language of the Church in the East at that time. In the year 381 it was expanded in **Constantinople**. This so-called **Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed** is accepted by almost all churches, including the Orthodox ones.

Later the Western Church added the Latin word **Filioque** to the creed. It means “and from the Son”. By this it is said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Eastern Church rejected this addition. The dispute contributed to the split between the Eastern and Western churches in the year 1054.

gewusst: The Nicene Creed has also been set to music by many great composers in their Masses.
The word symbolum originally meant a sign of recognition, for example a broken piece that fits exactly with the other.

teile.einleitung: Mendicant orders are Christian orders that arose in the 13th century. Their members wanted to live in poverty and live on donations. Instead of in remote monasteries, they worked mainly in the towns.
wichtigste: The technical term for mendicant orders is mendicants, from the Latin word for “to beg”.
Mendicant orders arose in the 13th century.
They settled mainly in the growing towns.
The mendicant orders include the Franciscans and the Dominicans.
The Cistercians are not among the mendicant orders.
The female branch of the Franciscans is called the Poor Clares.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages many monasteries were rich and owned a lot of land. Some Christians, by contrast, wanted to live as **poor** as Jesus and his disciples. They owned nothing and lived on **donations**. That is why they are called **mendicant orders** or **mendicants**, from the Latin word for “to beg”. They arose in the **13th century**.

The mendicant orders settled mainly in the **growing towns**. Many people lived there, including many poor people. The friars **preached** in squares and in churches, cared for the sick and helped the needy. Many also went to the new universities. The **Cistercians**, by contrast, are not a mendicant order: they mostly built their monasteries away from towns, in the country.

The best-known mendicant order is the **Franciscans**, founded by **Francis of Assisi**. His companion **Clare of Assisi** founded the female branch, the **Poor Clares**. Another great mendicant order is the **Dominicans**, founded by Dominic. They devoted themselves especially to preaching and study. Later further orders such as the Carmelites and the Augustinian Hermits were added.

In Swiss towns too there were monasteries of the mendicant orders in the Middle Ages. Still well known today are the **Capuchins**. They arose in the 16th century as a branch of the Franciscans. In many Catholic places in Switzerland there are Capuchin monasteries. Their name comes from the pointed hood of their habit.

gewusst: The drink cappuccino is named after the brown colour of the Capuchin habit.
Franciscans often wear a cord as a belt, whose three knots recall their vows.

teile.einleitung: Apostolic succession is the idea that the office of bishop reaches back in an unbroken chain to the apostles. For the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches it is very important. The Reformed churches understand the succession of the apostles differently.
wichtigste: Succession means following on.
What is meant is the unbroken line of ordination of bishops since the apostles.
The First Letter of Clement, around AD 96, is regarded as an early witness to it.
Irenaeus of Lyon cited lists of bishops in the 2nd century.
After the Council of Nicaea, at least three bishops are supposed to carry out an ordination of a bishop.
In 1896 Pope Leo XIII declared Anglican ordinations invalid.
Reformed Christians understand the succession above all as faithfulness to the teaching of the apostles.

abschnitte.titel: A chain back to the apostles
abschnitte.text: The word **succession** means **following on**. Bishops are ordained by other bishops through the **laying on of hands**. In this way an unbroken chain is meant to reach back to the **apostles**. This idea is especially important in the **Catholic**, **Orthodox** and **Anglican** churches. In their understanding, the line of ordination ensures that an office is lawful.

An early writing from Rome, around **AD 96**, is the **First Letter of Clement**. It is ascribed to **Clement of Rome**. The letter to the congregation in Corinth says that the apostles had appointed successors. In the **2nd century**, **Irenaeus of Lyon** named the bishops of Rome since the apostles in his work “Against Heresies”. He wanted to show that the true teaching was secured by this succession, and in this way he turned against the **Gnostics**.

The **Council of Nicaea** in the year 325 laid down rules for the ordination of bishops. According to **Canon 4**, if possible all the bishops of a province should take part, but at least **three**. This rule still applies in many churches today. It is meant to prevent a single bishop from appointing new bishops alone.

Not all churches recognise one another. In **1896**, Pope **Leo XIII** declared Anglican ordinations invalid with the bull **Apostolicae curae**. The Anglican Church rejected this. With the **Porvoo Declaration** of **1992**, Anglicans and Nordic Lutherans recognise one another's offices of bishop. It is named after the Finnish town of Porvoo.

In **1889**, Old Catholic churches joined together in the **Union of Utrecht**. This includes the **Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland**. These churches have bishops in apostolic succession. The **Reformed** churches see it differently. For **Zwingli** and **Calvin**, agreement with the **Gospel** counts for more than a historical line of ordination. People speak of a succession in **teaching**.

gewusst: From the 18th century the Archdiocese of Utrecht passed on its ordinations of bishops independently and without the consent of the pope.
The Catholic Church recognises the ordinations of bishops in the Orthodox churches as valid.

teile.einleitung: The Arian controversy was a great dispute in the early Church in the 4th century. It was about the question of whether Jesus Christ, as Son of God, is fully divine. The dispute shaped the Christian creed to this day.
wichtigste: The dispute started with the presbyter Arius in Alexandria.
Arius taught that the Son was a creature and not eternal like the Father.
The Council of Nicaea called the Son “homoousios”, that is, of the same being as the Father.
Athanasius was the most important opponent of the Arians.
Emperor Theodosius I made the Nicene faith binding in 380.
The Council of Constantinople in 381 largely ended the dispute in the empire.
Wulfila spread a Christianity with an Arian character among the Goths.

abschnitte.text: **Arius** was a priest, a so-called **presbyter**, in **Alexandria** in Egypt. Around **318** he fell into a dispute with his bishop, Alexander. Arius taught that the Son of God had been **created** by the Father. There had been a time when the Son was not. In this way he questioned the full **divinity** of Christ. Many Christians contradicted him fiercely.

In the year **325**, Emperor **Constantine** summoned the bishops to the **Council of Nicaea**. The council agreed a creed. In it, it says that the Son is **homoousios**, that is, **of the same being** as the Father. This Greek term was aimed directly against the teaching of Arius. But the dispute was far from over.

The most important opponent of the Arians was **Athanasius**, Bishop of Alexandria. He defended the creed of Nicaea all his life. But the emperors changed, and some supported the Arians. So Athanasius was sent into **exile** **five times**. Even so he did not give up, and was later honoured as a Church Father.

In **380** in Thessalonica, Emperor **Theodosius I** issued the edict **“Cunctos populos”**. With it the Nicene faith became binding for all inhabitants of the empire. In **381** the **First Council of Constantinople** confirmed the creed of Nicaea. It expanded the creed above all with statements about the **Holy Spirit**. In this way the **Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed** came about, which many churches still say today.

Outside the empire, Arianism lived on for a long time. In the 4th century Bishop **Wulfila** translated the Bible into **Gothic**. For this he created a script of his own. Through his mission many **Germanic** peoples at first became Arian Christians. The Frankish king **Clovis I**, by contrast, had himself baptised a **Catholic** around 500. In this way he won the support of the Gallo-Roman bishops and joined Franks and Gallo-Romans.

gewusst: A famous copy of Wulfila's Bible is the “Silver Codex” in Uppsala, written with silver ink on purple parchment.
The Burgundians too, who settled in western Switzerland in the 5th century, were at first Arian Christians.

teile.einleitung: The Diocese Article was a provision in the Swiss Federal Constitution. It laid down that new dioceses could be established only with the approval of the Confederation. In 2001 it was repealed in a popular vote.
wichtigste: The Diocese Article came with the total revision of the Federal Constitution in 1874.
New dioceses could be established only with the approval of the Confederation.
It is regarded as a relic of the Kulturkampf.
It was a reaction to an attempt by the Vatican to establish a diocese in Geneva.
In 1876 it was applied to the Christian Catholic diocese.
In 2001 it was repealed with almost two thirds voting yes.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century there was fierce conflict in Switzerland and other countries between the state and the Catholic Church. This conflict is called the **Kulturkampf**. The liberal politicians wanted to push back the influence of the pope. At that time the Vatican tried to establish a **diocese** of its own in **Geneva**. Many Swiss saw this as interference from outside.

With the **total revision of 1874**, Switzerland received a new Federal Constitution. In it stood the **Diocese Article**: dioceses could be established only with the **approval of the Confederation**. The constitution contained further provisions against the Catholic Church, for example the **ban on the Jesuits**. Such rules are called **denominational exceptional articles**.

The Diocese Article was applied only a single time. In **1876** the **Christian Catholic diocese** of Switzerland was established. The Christian Catholics had separated from Rome because they rejected new teachings of the pope. Their bishop has his seat in Bern. For new Roman Catholic dioceses, no approval under this article was ever given.

Little by little the exceptional articles were abolished. The ban on the Jesuits was struck out as early as **1973**. The people repealed the Diocese Article in a vote in the year **2001**, **with almost two thirds voting yes**. Since **2009**, in the same place, in **Article 72, paragraph 3**, stands the **ban on building minarets**. It was adopted by a popular initiative.

gewusst: The repeal required a majority of the people and of the cantons, because it was a change to the constitution.
Article 72 of the present Federal Constitution also says that the cantons are responsible for the relationship between church and state.

teile.einleitung: John the Baptist was a preacher at the time of Jesus. He lived in the wilderness, called people to repent and baptised them in the Jordan, including Jesus himself.
wichtigste: His parents were called Zechariah and Elizabeth.
He preached in the wilderness and is therefore called the “voice crying in the wilderness”.
He wore a garment of camel's hair and ate locusts and wild honey.
He is called the Baptist because he baptised many people.
He said of Jesus: “The one who comes after me is stronger than I.”
His feast day, Midsummer Day, is on 24 June.

abschnitte.text: John was the son of **Zechariah** and **Elizabeth**. Zechariah was a priest at the Temple in Jerusalem. The parents were already old and had had no children for a long time. Elizabeth was a relative of Mary, the mother of Jesus. So, according to the Bible, John and Jesus were related to each other.

As an adult John lived in the **wilderness** by the Jordan. He wore a **garment of camel's hair** with a leather belt. He ate **locusts and wild honey**. Because he preached there, he is also called the **voice crying in the wilderness**. This expression comes from the Book of Isaiah and is applied to him in the Gospels.

John called on people to **change their lives** and turn to God again. Many came to him, confessed their faults and were baptised in the **Jordan**. That is why he is called **the Baptist**. Baptism was a sign of a new beginning. Jesus too was baptised by John.

John saw himself as a forerunner. He said: “The one who comes after me is **stronger than I**.” He did not even feel worthy to carry his sandals. In many pictures John therefore points a finger at Jesus. Later the ruler **Herod Antipas** had him arrested and executed, because John had publicly criticised him.

The feast day of John, **Midsummer Day** (Johannistag), is on **24 June**. It falls about half a year before Christmas and close to the longest day of the year. In some regions fires are lit on this day. The **currant** (Johannisbeere in German) gets its name because it ripens around this time. In Switzerland many churches are named after John the Baptist.

gewusst: John the Baptist is venerated in Islam as the prophet Yahya.
The name John means “God is gracious”.

teile.einleitung: Gothic is a medieval building style that arose in the 12th century in **France**. Gothic cathedrals are tall, bright and full of coloured glass windows. Typical features are **pointed arches**, flying buttresses and large rose windows.
wichtigste: The Gothic style arose in France.
The abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris is regarded as the first Gothic building.
Typical features are pointed arches and flying buttresses on the outside of the walls.
Large round windows are called rose windows.
Gargoyles carry rainwater away from the roof.
Cologne Cathedral was only completed in 1880.

abschnitte.text: The Gothic style began around the year 1140 in **France**. The **abbey church of Saint-Denis** near Paris is regarded as the first Gothic building. Abbot Suger had it rebuilt because he wanted a brighter church. The new style soon spread throughout Europe. It replaced the Romanesque style with its thick walls and round arches.

The most important distinguishing feature is the **pointed arch**. It carries weight downwards better than a round arch. On the outside, **flying buttresses** support the walls; these are piers and arches that take up the pressure. This meant the walls could be thinner and have large windows. The churches thus became much taller and brighter.

Many cathedrals have a **rose window**, a large round window with stone **tracery**. The coloured glass windows often show stories from the Bible. On the roof sit **gargoyles**, which lead rainwater away from the walls. They are often shaped as fabulous creatures or grotesque faces. In this way the masonry was protected from damp.

**Cologne Cathedral** was begun in 1248 and was only completed in **1880**, after over 600 years. **Ulm Minster**, at about 161 metres, has the tallest church tower in the world. At **Notre-Dame de Paris**, the roof burned in **2019**, after which the cathedral was painstakingly restored. In Switzerland, for example, **Bern Minster** and **Lausanne Cathedral** are Gothic.

gewusst: The name Gothic was originally meant as an insult: later artists regarded the style as barbaric like the Goths.
The tower of Bern Minster is the tallest church tower in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Eucharist is one of the most important celebrations in Christianity. It recalls the last meal of Jesus with his disciples. In the Catholic Church it is the centre of the Mass.
wichtigste: “Eucharist” is Greek and means thanksgiving.
At Communion the host is given out, a thin, round piece of bread.
Consecrated hosts are kept in the tabernacle.
The Eternal Light shows that there are consecrated hosts in the tabernacle.
The vessel for the hosts is called a ciborium.
The words “This is my body” are called the words of institution.

abschnitte.text: The Greek word **Eucharist** means **thanksgiving**. At the last meal, Jesus thanked God for bread and wine. That is why the celebration has this name. In the Catholic and Orthodox churches people speak of the Eucharist, in the Protestant churches usually of the **Lord's Supper**.

At Mass and at the Lord's Supper the words of Jesus are spoken: “This is my body” and “This is my blood”. They are called the **words of institution**, because with them Jesus instituted the celebration. The churches understand them differently. According to Catholic teaching, bread and wine really become the body and blood of Christ. The Reformed churches in Switzerland, following Zwingli, understand the meal more as a remembrance.

In the Catholic Church the **host** is given out at Communion. It is a thin, round bread made of flour and water, without leaven. The hosts are kept and handed out in a vessel with a lid, the **ciborium**. Catholics should eat nothing for **an hour** before receiving Communion. Water and medicines are allowed.

Consecrated hosts that are left over go into the **tabernacle**. This is a decorated, lockable cupboard in the church. Next to it burns the **Eternal Light**, usually a red lamp. It shows that there are consecrated hosts in the tabernacle. That is why many believers briefly kneel in front of it.

gewusst: The word “host” comes from the Latin “hostia” and means a sacrificial offering.
The word “tabernacle” originally means tent or hut.

teile.einleitung: Christianity has a very long history in Africa. Even in the first centuries there were Christians in Egypt, Ethiopia and North Africa. Today, according to estimates, more Christians live in Africa than on any other continent.
wichtigste: Christianity has existed in North Africa, Egypt and Ethiopia since the first centuries.
Since about 2018, Africa has had the most Christians of all continents, according to estimates.
African independent churches were founded without European mission churches.
The Kimbanguist Church goes back to a prophet who began his work in 1921.
Samuel Ajayi Crowther became the first African Anglican bishop in 1864.
Desmond Tutu received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984.

abschnitte.text: Christianity reached Africa very early. In **Egypt** the Coptic Church came into being, and in **Ethiopia** Christianity became the state religion in the 4th century. There were also many Christians in North Africa. **Augustine**, Bishop of Hippo in what is now Algeria, is famous. The churches in Egypt and Ethiopia still exist today.

From the 19th century onwards, many missionaries came from Europe and America to other parts of Africa. Soon Africans themselves took on offices in the churches. **Samuel Ajayi Crowther** from what is now Nigeria became the first African bishop of the **Anglican Church** in **1864**. In **Uganda**, young Christians were killed between 1885 and 1887 under King **Mwanga II**. They are honoured as the Martyrs of Uganda.

Many Africans founded their own churches, independent of the European mission churches. They are called **African independent churches**. There, Christian faith and African traditions come together, for example in dance and music. The **Kimbanguist Church** is named after the prophet Simon Kimbangu, who began his work in **1921** in what was then the Belgian Congo. In South Africa the **Zion Christian Church** is the largest independent church.

For a long time South Africa was ruled by **apartheid**, a policy of separating Black and white people. The Anglican clergyman **Desmond Tutu** fought against it without violence. For this he received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in **1984**. Later he became Archbishop of Cape Town. After apartheid ended, he worked for reconciliation.

The number of Christians in Africa grew strongly in the 20th century. According to estimates by church statisticians, Africa has had the **most Christians** of all continents since about **2018**. In **Ivory Coast** stands the Basilica of **Our Lady of Peace** (Notre-Dame de la Paix), one of the largest churches in the world. In the north of Africa, by contrast, Islam is the main religion.

gewusst: The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro is modelled on St Peter's Basilica in Rome.
Even in the Acts of the Apostles in the Bible, an official from Ethiopia is baptised.

teile.einleitung: Jan Hus was a Czech theologian and preacher in Prague. He criticised abuses in the Church and was condemned and burned at the Council of Constance in 1415. In the Czech Republic he is still honoured as a national hero.
wichtigste: Jan Hus was ordained a priest in the year 1400.
In the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague he preached in Czech.
In 1410 he was excommunicated.
The Council of Constance condemned him, in 1415 he was burned and his ashes scattered in the Rhine.
A year later his friend Jerome of Prague also died in Constance.
His day of death, 6 July, has been a public holiday in the Czech Republic since 1925.

abschnitte.text: Jan Hus was born around 1370 in Bohemia. He studied in Prague and later taught at the university. In the year **1400** he was **ordained a priest**. From 1402 he preached in the **Bethlehem Chapel** in Prague. There he spoke not Latin but **Czech**, so that all the people understood him. Very many people often listened to him.

Hus was influenced by the writings of the Englishman John Wycliffe. He criticised the fact that many clergy were rich and that Church offices were sold. He said that the Bible must stand above everything, even above the Pope. In particular he opposed the sale of **indulgences**. In **1410** he was **excommunicated**, that is, shut out of the Church.

In 1414 Hus travelled to the **Council of Constance** on Lake Constance, right on the border of present-day Switzerland. King Sigismund had promised him safe conduct. Even so he was taken prisoner and accused as a heretic. He refused to recant his teachings. On **6 July 1415** he was burned, and his **ashes were scattered in the Rhine**. In 1416 his friend **Jerome of Prague** died in the same way.

Hus also cared about the **Czech language**. He is credited with having introduced the spelling with **marks above letters**. In this way a sound can be written with one letter, such as č. These little hooks and strokes shape the Czech script to this day. Later they were also adopted by other languages.

After the death of Hus, the **Hussite Wars** broke out in Bohemia. Many see him as a forerunner of the Reformation. On the **Old Town Square** in Prague stands a large **Jan Hus Memorial**. His day of death has been a **public holiday** in the Czech Republic since **1925**. In Constance the **Hus Stone** recalls the place of his execution.

gewusst: The name Hus means “goose” in Czech.
In Constance there is a Hus Museum in the house where he is said to have lived.

teile.einleitung: In the parable of the house builders, Jesus tells of two men who each build a house. One builds on **rock**, the other on **sand**. When a storm comes, it is shown who built wisely.
wichtigste: The wise man builds his house on rock.
The foolish man builds his house on sand.
Rain, floods and wind strike both houses.
The house on the rock stays standing, the one on the sand collapses.
The wise man stands for someone who hears the words of Jesus and acts on them.
Jesus tells the parable at the end of the Sermon on the Mount.

abschnitte.text: A **parable** is a short story with a deeper meaning. In this parable a **wise** man builds his house on solid rock. A **foolish**, that is, stupid, man builds his house on sand. From the outside both houses perhaps look the same. The difference lies in the **foundation**, that is, the ground on which a house stands.

One day heavy **rain**, **floods** and **wind** come. They strike both houses with full force. The house on the rock **stays standing**, because its ground is firm. The house on the sand **collapses**, and its fall is great. Now it can be seen who made good preparations.

Jesus himself explains what he means. The wise man is like someone who **hears and does** his words. The foolish man is like someone who hears them but does **not live by them**. So it is not enough just to listen. Whoever also acts on them has a firm foundation for difficult times in life.

abschnitte.titel: Where it is in the Bible
abschnitte.text: The parable is found in the **Gospel of Matthew** at the end of the **Sermon on the Mount**, the great speech of Jesus. There is also a version in the **Gospel of Luke**. There it says that the wise man **digs deep** before laying the foundation on the rock. The parable is often told in religious education and in children's songs.

gewusst: Even today a firm foundation is important for every house, especially on slopes in the mountains.
The Sermon on the Mount also contains the Lord's Prayer.

teile.einleitung: Jeremias Gotthelf was a pastor and one of the best-known Swiss writers. His real name was Albert Bitzius, and he wrote about the life of farmers in the Emmental.
wichtigste: Albert Bitzius was born in 1797 in Murten as the son of a pastor.
From 1832 he was pastor in Lützelflüh in the Emmental.
His first novel “Der Bauernspiegel” (The Farmers' Mirror) appeared in 1837.
He took the name Jeremias Gotthelf from the first-person narrator of this novel.
His most famous novella is “The Black Spider”.
He campaigned especially for the poor and for Verdingkinder (indentured children).

abschnitte.text: **Albert Bitzius** was born in 1797 in **Murten**. His father was a pastor, and he too studied theology in Bern. From **1832** he was pastor in **Lützelflüh** in the Emmental. There he got to know the life of the farmers, maids and farmhands closely. He stayed in this parish until his death in 1854.

In 1837 his first novel **“Der Bauernspiegel”** appeared. The first-person narrator in it is called **Jeremias Gotthelf** and tells of his hard life as a poor boy. From then on Bitzius published his books under this name. He wrote a great deal about the misery of the poor and of the **Verdingkinder**. These were children who had to work for strange farmers and were often badly treated.

Gotthelf's most famous story is **“The Black Spider”** of 1842. In it villagers, out of need, make a pact with the devil, who appears as the **Green Huntsman**. Because they break their promise, a black spider comes over the village and brings death and ruin. In the end the spider is **shut up in a window post** and sealed with a plug. The story is regarded as one of the most important narratives in the German language.

In the novel **“Uli der Knecht”** (Uli the Farmhand), Gotthelf tells of a young farmhand. Uli at first lives carelessly, but through **diligence and faith** finds his way to an orderly life. The sequel “Uli der Pächter” (Uli the Tenant) followed later. The books show farming life very precisely. Gotthelf did not want only to entertain his readers, but also to educate them.

In 1837 a severe **flood disaster** struck the Emmental. Gotthelf described it in the story **“Die Wassernot im Emmental”** (The Flood in the Emmental). He portrayed how the Emme and its streams destroyed houses, bridges and fields. Gotthelf's books were later often filmed, for example “Uli der Knecht” in the 1950s. In Lützelflüh the **Gotthelf Centre** now recalls him.

gewusst: Gotthelf put many Bernese German words into his standard German texts so that they felt authentic.
Albert Bitzius was also a school inspector and looked after the schools in his area.

teile.einleitung: Harvest Thanksgiving is a Christian festival in autumn. People thank God for the harvest and for everything that has grown in fields, meadows and trees. At the same time the festival reminds us to share food.
wichtigste: At Harvest Thanksgiving, Christians thank God for the harvest.
It is celebrated in autumn, mostly in September or October.
Fruit, vegetables, grain and bread are laid out in front of the altar.
A harvest crown is a decoration made of ears of grain.
After the festival, the gifts are often given to people in need.
People also think of the work of farmers.

abschnitte.text: In autumn most of the harvest has been brought in. That is why many churches celebrate **Harvest Thanksgiving** in September or October. In Catholic and Protestant congregations it is often a Sunday in autumn. There is no fixed day for all churches. The service is usually especially cheerful and festive.

Christians believe that **God** created the world. That is why they thank him for sun, rain and good growth. They know that food cannot be taken for granted. A good harvest depends on the weather and can also fail. The festival invites us to be grateful for what we have.

In front of the **altar** people lay apples, pumpkins, potatoes, grain and bread. In this way you can see how rich the harvest is. The **pumpkin** is a typical autumn vegetable, big and orange. The **bread** recalls the grain from which flour is made. Often a **harvest crown** also hangs in the church. It is made from bound ears of grain and decorated with ribbons and flowers.

Farmers sow, tend and harvest. Their work is often hard and depends on the weather. At Harvest Thanksgiving, people therefore also think of them. In some Swiss villages there are processions with decorated carts or a market for the festival.

Many parishes give the food away after the festival to **people in need**. In this way the harvest is shared. Sometimes the gifts go to aid organisations or to places where people can shop cheaply. The festival reminds us that not everyone has enough to eat.

gewusst: Harvest festivals existed long before Christianity, for example among the ancient Romans and Greeks.
Judaism also has a harvest festival: the Feast of Tabernacles, Sukkot, in autumn.

teile.einleitung: Jacob and Esau are two brothers from the first book of the Bible. Their story tells of quarrel, cunning and flight, but in the end also of reconciliation.
wichtigste: Jacob and Esau were twins.
Their parents were called Isaac and Rebekah.
Esau was a hunter, while Jacob preferred to stay by the tents.
Esau sold his birthright for a dish of lentils.
Disguised with goatskins, Jacob tricked his way to the blessing of his blind father.
In the end the brothers were reconciled.

abschnitte.text: The story is in the book of **Genesis**, the first book of Moses. **Isaac** and **Rebekah** had two sons, the **twins** Esau and Jacob. Esau was the elder, he was very hairy and liked to **go hunting**. Jacob was quieter and preferred to stay by the tents. The father favoured Esau, the mother Jacob.

As the eldest son, Esau had the **birthright**. This meant that he would later inherit more and lead the family. One day Esau came home hungry from hunting. Jacob was just cooking a red **lentil stew**. Esau wanted some of it, and Jacob demanded his birthright for it. Esau was so hungry that he agreed.

When Isaac was old and **blind**, he wanted to bless Esau. The mother **Rebekah** heard this and helped Jacob with a **trick**. Jacob put on Esau's clothes and wrapped **goatskins** around his hands and neck. In this way he felt hairy like his brother. Isaac let himself be deceived and gave Jacob the blessing. When Esau found out, he was very angry.

abschnitte.titel: Flight and the ladder to heaven
abschnitte.text: Jacob had to flee from his brother and went to his uncle Laban. On the way he slept under the open sky with a stone as a pillow. In a **dream** he saw a **ladder up to heaven**, on which angels were going up and down. God promised to accompany him. Jacob called the place Bethel, which means “house of God”.

After many years with Laban, Jacob returned with his family and large herds. He was afraid of Esau and sent gifts ahead of him. But Esau ran to meet him, embraced him and wept. The brothers were **reconciled**. Jacob was later given the name **Israel**, and the name of the people of Israel derives from him.

gewusst: The expression “to sell for a mess of pottage” still means today to give up something valuable for a trifle.
Jacob's dream gave its name to the ladder to heaven, which is also called “Jacob's ladder”.

teile.einleitung: The Peace of Augsburg was an imperial law in the Holy Roman Empire. It was agreed on 25 September 1555 and regulated how Catholics and Lutherans lived together.
wichtigste: The Peace of Augsburg was agreed on 25 September 1555 at the Imperial Diet of Augsburg.
It recognised Catholics and Lutherans under imperial law.
The ruler of a territory determined the denomination of his territory.
Later this was summed up in the formula “cuius regio, eius religio”.
Subjects of another denomination were allowed to emigrate.
King Ferdinand I negotiated in place of Emperor Charles V.

abschnitte.text: After the **Reformation** the empire was split into Catholics and Protestants. Many princes had adopted the Lutheran teaching. Emperor **Charles V** wanted to preserve unity of faith. In 1546 and 1547 he fought the **Schmalkaldic War** against Protestant princes and won it. But with this he could not settle the dispute over faith.

In 1555 the estates of the empire met in **Augsburg**. Charles V did not want to sign a peace with the Protestants himself. So his brother, King **Ferdinand I**, negotiated in his place. On **25 September 1555** the religious peace was agreed. For the time being it ended the wars of religion in the empire.

The peace recognised two denominations: **Catholics** and **Lutherans**. Every ruler was allowed to decide which of them applied in his territory. Later this principle was summed up in the Latin formula **“cuius regio, eius religio”**, in English “whose region, his religion”. Subjects who had a different faith received the **right to emigrate**.

A special rule applied to spiritual princes, that is, bishops and abbots who were also rulers of territories. If they changed to the Lutheran teaching, they lost **office and rule**. This was called the **ecclesiastical reservation**. In this way the spiritual territories were to remain Catholic. The Protestants rejected this rule.

The **Reformed**, that is, the followers of Zwingli and Calvin, were not included. The freedom of individual people to choose their faith did not yet exist either. The tensions remained and later contributed to the **Thirty Years' War**. Only the **Peace of Westphalia** of 1648 recognised the Reformed as well.

gewusst: The Swiss Confederation was not affected by the Peace of Augsburg. There, its own Landfrieden regulated the relationship between the denominations.
The peace lasted in the empire for over 60 years before the Thirty Years' War began in 1618.

teile.einleitung: The altar is the most important table in a church. It stands at the front, and at it bread and wine are prepared for communion or Mass. Altars come in many forms, from plain to splendid.
wichtigste: An altar usually looks like a big table made of stone or wood.
It stands at the front of the church, in the so-called chancel.
At the altar, bread and wine are prepared for communion or Mass.
A white cloth often lies on the altar.
A cross often stands on or above the altar.
In Reformed churches people often speak of the communion table.
A winged altarpiece has picture panels that fold open.

abschnitte.text: An **altar** is like a big table made of **stone** or **wood**. It stands at the **front** of the church, and all the pews face in its direction. The front part of the church is called the **chancel**. The altar stands there, often raised a little on steps. In this way everyone can see it well.

At the altar, bread and wine are prepared and shared at **communion** or at **Mass**. In this way Christians remember the last meal of Jesus with his disciples. A white **altar cloth** often lies on the altar. It shows that the altar is a special place. On or above the altar there is often a **cross**, which recalls Jesus. Candles and sometimes flowers are added.

In **Catholic** churches the altar is often made of stone and richly decorated. In **Reformed** churches people usually speak of the **communion table**. It is plainer and often made of wood. The reformers such as **Zwingli** wanted simplicity instead of show. That is why many Reformed churches in Switzerland are rather plain inside.

A **winged altarpiece** is an altar with painted or carved wooden panels. The side panels, the **wings**, can be folded open and shut. On ordinary days the altarpiece stays closed. On **feast days** it is opened to show the most beautiful pictures. Winged altarpieces were especially popular in the **late Middle Ages**.

Altars existed long before Christianity. Many ancient religions made **offerings** to their gods on altars. In the Bible too, people such as Noah or Abraham build altars out of stones. The word **altar** comes from Latin and means a raised place for offerings.

gewusst: In many Catholic altars there are relics, that is, remains of saints, set into them.
One of the most famous winged altarpieces is the Isenheim Altarpiece in Colmar in Alsace.

teile.einleitung: The Exodus from Egypt is one of the most important stories of the Bible. It tells how Moses led the people of Israel out of oppression in Egypt. The story is in the Book of Exodus, whose name in Greek means “going out”.
wichtigste: Moses led the people of Israel out of Egypt.
The army of Pharaoh pursued the Israelites as far as the sea.
When Moses stretched out his hand, the sea parted.
A strong east wind drove the water back all night.
By day a pillar of cloud showed the way.
Miriam played the tambourine and sang a song of thanks.
The Jewish festival of Passover recalls the Exodus.

abschnitte.text: According to the Bible, the Israelites lived in **Egypt** for a long time. **Pharaoh**, the king of Egypt, forced them to do hard labour. God commissioned **Moses** to lead the people to freedom. But Pharaoh did not want to let the Israelites go. Only after heavy plagues came upon Egypt did he give way.

The Israelites had scarcely left when Pharaoh regretted his decision. He sent his **army** after them, as far as the sea. Moses stretched his hand out over the water. A **strong east wind** drove the sea back all night, and it **parted**. The people went through on dry ground. When the Egyptians followed, the **water rushed back**.

On the way through the desert, according to the story, God was always with his people. By day a **pillar of cloud** went before them and showed the way. By night a **pillar of fire** shone. In this way they could travel day and night. These images show that God leads and protects the people.

After the rescue, Moses and the Israelites sang a song of thanks. **Miriam**, the sister of Moses and Aaron, took a **tambourine** in her hand. The women followed her, dancing and singing. This song is among the oldest texts of the Bible. Then the people travelled on through the desert to Mount Sinai, where they received the **Ten Commandments**.

Every spring Jews celebrate the festival of **Passover**. It recalls the liberation from Egypt. On the first evening there is a festive meal, the **Seder**. People eat unleavened bread, the **matzah**, because the Israelites had no time to let the dough rise. The Christian festival of Easter also has its roots in Passover.

gewusst: According to the Bible, the journey through the desert lasted 40 years.
At the Seder, children traditionally ask why this evening is different from all other evenings.

teile.einleitung: The resurrection of Jesus Christ is the most important article of faith in Christianity. The Bible tells that after his death on the cross, Jesus became alive again on the third day. Christians recall this every year at Easter.
wichtigste: According to the Bible, Jesus died on Good Friday and was laid in a tomb.
On the third day, a Sunday, women found the tomb empty.
According to the Gospel of John, Mary Magdalene was the first to meet the risen Jesus.
The two disciples of Emmaus recognised Jesus at the breaking of bread.
Jesus greeted the disciples with the words “Peace be with you”.
Easter is the highest festival of Christians.

abschnitte.text: According to the account in the Gospels, Jesus died on **Good Friday** and was buried. Early in the morning on the first day of the week, that is, on **Sunday**, women went to the tomb. They had bought **fragrant oils** to anoint the dead man, as was the custom then. But the tomb was **empty**. According to the Gospel of Mark, they heard there that Jesus was going ahead of the disciples to **Galilee**, and that there they would see him.

The Gospel of John tells of **Mary Magdalene**. She stood weeping by the tomb and saw a man whom she took for the **gardener**. Only when he called her by name did she recognise Jesus. In this way, according to this account, she became the first witness of the resurrection. She ran to the disciples and told them about it.

The Gospel of Luke tells of two disciples who were walking to Emmaus. A stranger walked with them and spoke with them about the scriptures. They did not recognise him. Only in the evening at the meal, when he **broke the bread**, did they realise that it was Jesus. Then they hurried back to Jerusalem.

The disciples had shut themselves in out of fear. Then Jesus came and stood among them and said: “**Peace be with you!**” At first they thought they were seeing a ghost. According to Luke, Jesus therefore ate a **piece of broiled fish** before their eyes. In this the Gospels want to show that the risen Jesus really lived.

The resurrection is recalled by the **Easter festival**, the highest festival in the church year. Because the tomb was empty on a Sunday, **Sunday** is a special day for Christians. It is also called “the Lord's Day”. For Christians the resurrection means that death does not have the last word. Whether and how one believes in it is a question of personal faith.

gewusst: The date of Easter changes every year: Easter is on the first Sunday after the first full moon in spring.
The word “Hallelujah” is Hebrew and means “Praise God”. On Easter night it is sung with special solemnity.

teile.einleitung: “The Last Supper” is a famous wall painting by Leonardo da Vinci in Milan. It shows Jesus with his twelve apostles at their last meal together. The picture is among the best-known works of art of the Renaissance.
wichtigste: Leonardo da Vinci painted the picture from about 1494 to 1498.
It was commissioned by the Duke of Milan, Ludovico Sforza.
The picture is painted on the wall of the dining hall in the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie.
It shows the moment when Jesus says that one of them will betray him.
Twelve apostles sit in four groups of three beside Jesus.
Leonardo painted on dry plaster, so the paint soon began to flake off.
All the lines of the perspective run towards the head of Jesus.

abschnitte.titel: A picture in the dining hall
abschnitte.text: The **Last Supper** is in the **refectory**, that is, the dining hall, of the monastery of **Santa Maria delle Grazie** in Milan. The commission was given by Duke **Ludovico Sforza**. Leonardo worked on it from about **1494 to 1498**. The monks ate here, as it were, together with Jesus and the disciples. The picture is very large, measuring about 4.6 by 8.8 metres.

Leonardo painted the moment when Jesus says: “One of you will betray me.” The **apostles** react with shock and excitement, some jumping up, others asking questions. Jesus sits calmly in the middle. To his right and left sit six apostles each, arranged in **four groups of three people**. This makes the scene lively and yet orderly.

**Judas** can be recognised by a small **bag** that he clutches. It recalls the silver coins he received for the betrayal. His face is also in **shadow**. Unlike many painters before him, Leonardo did not place Judas alone on the other side of the table, but among the other apostles.

Leonardo used **central perspective**. All the lines of the ceiling and walls run towards one point, the so-called vanishing point. It lies exactly at the **head of Jesus**. In this way the viewer's gaze is led quite naturally to the centre. The bright window behind Jesus also makes him stand out.

Leonardo did not paint as a **fresco** in wet plaster. He experimented with **tempera** on a dry wall so that he could work slowly. But the paint did not stick well and soon began to flake. Over the centuries the picture was restored many times. The last major restoration lasted from 1978 to 1999.

gewusst: In the Second World War a bomb hit the monastery in 1943, but the wall with the Last Supper remained standing.
The monastery with the Last Supper has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980.

teile.einleitung: Huldrych Zwingli was the most important Reformer of German-speaking Switzerland. From Zurich he changed church and faith and shaped the Reformed church to this day.
wichtigste: Zwingli was born in 1484 in Wildhaus in the Toggenburg.
From 1519 he was people's priest at the Grossmünster in Zurich.
In 1523, at the First Zurich Disputation, he presented 67 Theses.
The council of the city of Zurich decided on the introduction of the Reformation.
In 1525 the Mass was replaced in Zurich by the Lord's Supper.
Zwingli died in 1531 in the Battle of Kappel, and his successor was Heinrich Bullinger.

abschnitte.text: Zwingli was born on 1 January 1484 in **Wildhaus** in the Toggenburg. He studied in Vienna and Basel and became a priest. At first he worked in Glarus, then as a people's priest in **Einsiedeln**. From 1519 he was **people's priest at the Grossmünster** in Zurich. A people's priest is the priest responsible for preaching and pastoral care for the ordinary people.

In Zurich, Zwingli preached continuously from the Bible, chapter by chapter. He was convinced that only what is in **Holy Scripture** counts. In 1522 some of his followers publicly broke the fasting rule, at the well-known **Affair of the Sausages**. Zwingli defended them. With this the open quarrel with the old church began.

In January 1523 the **First Zurich Disputation** took place, a public debate. For it Zwingli presented **67 Theses**, that is, statements of teaching about the faith. It was not the bishop who was allowed to decide, but the **city council**. The council sided with Zwingli. After that images were removed from the churches and monasteries were dissolved, and in **1525** the Mass was replaced by the **Lord's Supper**.
